title: The Evolution of Exchange: From Barter Frictions to Decentralized AI Infrastructures: Transaction Costs, Intermediation, and the Political Economy of AI-Mediated Commerce

detail.title: The Evolution of Exchange: From Barter Frictions to Decentralized AI Infrastructures: Transaction Costs, Intermediation, and the Political Economy of AI-Mediated Commerce
detail.abstract: This paper is a conceptual and historical analysis intended to clarify the structural relationship between transaction-cost reduction, intermediation, and market power. It does not present an empirical model or testable hypotheses. The framework is intended to support analysis across multiple domains in which AI-mediated coordination plays an increasing role.

title: Lifecycle Optimization of Offshore Oil Infrastructure in African Operations

detail.title: Lifecycle Optimization of Offshore Oil Infrastructure in African Operations
detail.abstract: Offshore oil infrastructure plays a critical role in Africa's energy production and economic development. However, operational inefficiencies, high maintenance costs, environmental risks, and aging infrastructure challenge optimal performance. This study explores lifecycle optimization strategies for offshore oil platforms in African operations, focusing on predictive maintenance, digital tools, cost management, and environmental sustainability. The methodology integrates literature review, optimization model assessment, and analysis of digital monitoring techniques. Findings indicate that lifecycle optimization reduces operational downtime, improves cost efficiency, and mitigates environmental impacts. Furthermore, the adoption of smart asset management and real-time monitoring enhances safety and operational reliability. The study concludes that applying tailored lifecycle optimization strategies is essential for sustainable and economically viable offshore operations in Africa, highlighting the need for region-specific models and further research into digital integration and climate adaptation.

title: The Inevitability of Marbury v. Madison
affiliations: Israel Supreme Court

detail.title: The Inevitability of Marbury v. Madison

publicationDetails.detailsText: ICL - Vienna Journal on International Constitutional Law (forthcoming in 2026)

detail.abstract:
This Article uncovers three pivotal insights from Marbury v. Madison, highlighting their universal significance and enduring relevance in contemporary constitutional practice. Specifically, it argues that Chief Justice Marshall’s reasoning in this landmark decision built up a distinctly positivist value-free conception of legality capable of resolving constitutional crises. Based on this argument, the Article positions Marbury v. Madison not only as a foundational precedent for judicial review in the United States but also as a precursor to modern constitutional practice worldwide.

The positivist insights extracted from Marshall’s decision include the following: (1) the treatment of law as a social fact; (2) the adoption of an “internal point of view” in interpreting legal texts; and (3) the identification of “secondary” power-conferring rules that derive from the foundational “rule of recognition.” The Article reveals that Marshall’s insights align remarkably with the principles of legal positivism articulated by H.L.A. Hart and his followers over 150 years later. The Article examines these insights in light of recent constitutional developments in Israel, where the author, as a Supreme Court Justice, applied Marshall’s jurisprudential framework to address fundamental questions that arose in connection with judicial review and constitutional amendments. This discussion goes beyond Israel’s borders: it demonstrates that Marshall’s positivist framework is essential for legitimizing judicial review and articulating the notion of “constitutionality.” By uncovering the conceptual necessity of this framework for all forms of judicial review, the Article brings to light the timeless and universal nature of the Marbury v. Madison decision, emphasizing its continued relevance in addressing contemporary constitutional challenges.

title: Switching Gradient: Learning to Compete with Price-Matching Guarantee
affiliations: Shanghai University of Finance and Economics, Northwestern University - Department of Industrial Engineering and Management Sciences,  and Shanghai University of Finance and Economics - School of Information Management and Engineering

detail.title: Switching Gradient: Learning to Compete with Price-Matching Guarantee
detail.abstract: Price-Matching Guarantee (PMG) has become a widespread strategy among retailers to attract and retain customers by promising to match lower prices. However, how sellers should dynamically set prices under PMG, especially without full knowledge of price competition, remains unclear. We model online price competition in a duopoly market with asymmetric PMG adoption. Customers request refunds when the price difference exceeds their hassle threshold, thereby distorting both sellers' revenue functions. Each seller observes only their own realized demand and must learn to optimize on the fly without knowing the demand model or the other seller's information. The setting poses unique challenges, including discontinuous and non-convex revenue functions due to PMG, as well as biased and incomplete feedback arising from online competition. To address these challenges, we propose a novel switching gradient algorithm, in which the PMG provider alternates between real and artificial gradients based on a diagnostic function, while the other seller ignores PMG distortions in gradient estimation. Our algorithm achieves dynamic regret of order $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{T})$ for the PMG provider and $\mathcal{O}(\log T \sqrt{T})$ for the other seller, along with last-iterate convergence to the static Nash equilibrium at rate $\mathcal{O}(\log T / \sqrt{T})$. We introduce a new analytical framework to rigorously quantify regret and convergence rates under asymmetric knowledge and heterogeneous step sizes. For retailers adopting PMG or other pricing mechanisms that introduce discontinuities in revenue, our framework offers a practical way to adapt classical gradient-based learning algorithms to accommodate structural complexities. For sellers competing against PMG adopters, our findings indicate that conventional pricing policies may remain effective, even without adjustment to the new environment, and that the burden of adaptation lies primarily on the PMG provider. Furthermore, we demonstrate that improved revenue and convergence may not be achieved without additional information sharing, highlighting the ``Price of Non-Cooperation''.

title: Period Talk on the Factory Floor: Evidence from a Workplace Menstrual Awareness Campaign Involving Men
affiliations: Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU) and Ludwig Maximilian University of Munich (LMU)

detail.title: Period Talk on the Factory Floor: Evidence from a Workplace Menstrual Awareness Campaign Involving Men
detail.abstract: Menstruation is a common biological process that affects women at work, yet in many LMICs it is expected to be managed in private and is rarely considered when organizations address workers' needs. This paper studies a large-scale menstrual awareness campaign in a Bangladeshi garment factory, where short audio messages about menstruation were broadcast daily over factory loudspeakers and heard by both women and men. Using before-after survey data from a panel of workers, we show that men are already heavily involved in menstrual management prior to the campaign, with many reporting that they buy pads for their wives because they feel ashamed purchasing commercial absorbents themselves. Following the campaign, menstrual stigma and taboos decline for both women and men, and restrictive social norms become more permissive for behaviors related to cross-gender communication and purchasing menstrual products, while norms limiting the washing and drying of reusable absorbents remain more resistant to change. These findings suggest that low-cost, mixed-gender workplace campaigns can shift the social environment surrounding menstruation at scale, pointing to a feasible organizational strategy to reduce hidden, norm-driven barriers to women’s well-being and labor participation in low- and middle-income countries.

title: Geometric Cointegration and Rotor Dynamics in the Term Structure of Interest Rates
affiliations: GeometriX Intelligence and

detail.title: Geometric Cointegration and Rotor Dynamics in the Term Structure of Interest Rates
detail.abstract: We introduce geometric cointegration, a framework that replaces the classical fixed-vector projection of cointegration analysis with a time-varying unit normal vector governed by rotor dynamics on the unit sphere. Classical cointegration imposes a constant equilibrium hyperplane on a system of I(1) series, an assumption that may be empirically restrictive across the severaldecade horizons relevant to interest rate modelling. Our approach embeds the cointegrating vector on S d-1 and tracks its evolution through a sequence of minimal rotations, each parameterised by a scalar rotation angle α t calibrated via a penalised least-squares objective that balances fit against rotational inertia controlled by a smoothness hyperparameter λ > 0. Applied to 413 monthly observations of US Treasury yields (3-month, 2-year, and 10-year maturities) spanning January 1990 to May 2024, the framework reveals a yield-curve equilibrium that is geometrically stable yet structurally time-varying. In the 2-dimensional system pairing TB3MS and DGS10 (with λ = 5.0), the mean absolute rotation angle is 0.02042 radians (1.17 •), confirming that the equilibrium normal remains in a well-defined small-angle regime throughout the sample. The maximum absolute angle of 0.13022 radians (7.46 •) occurs during peak macrofinancial stress episodes. The equilibrium error u t = n ⊤ t z t exhibits a standard deviation of 0.1674 in standardised units, while the cointegrating direction ϕ t traces a total arc of 79.65 • across the 34-year sample. The 3-dimensional blade system incorporating the 2-year yield produces even smaller rotations (mean 1.10 • , maximum 5.61 •), consistent with the additional constraint imposed by a third maturity. We establish formally that in the small-angle limit the rotor correction reduces exactly to a classical error-correction mechanism (ECM), with the equilibrium error shrinking at rate λ/(B 2 t + λ) per period. As λ → ∞ the cointegrating vector freezes and the model collapses to standard Johansen cointegration. The hyperparameter λ therefore provides a continuous bridge between the two extremes. We further show that the squared rotation angle α * 2 t constitutes a natural geometric energy that spikes sharply at the Global Financial Crisis (2008-2009), the COVID-19 shock (2020), and the early-1990s monetary tightening episode-making it a potential real-time macro-stress indicator. Nelson-Siegel factor projections of the 3D blade reveal that the 1 slope direction dominates, consistent with the empirical primacy of the level-slope structure in term structure models.

title: Stimulating Auto Markets
affiliations: Duke University, Fuqua School of Business-Economics Group, Government of the Commonwealth of Australia - Department of the Treasury, Board of Governors of the Federal Reserve System and University of Chicago - Finance

detail.title: Stimulating Auto Markets
detail.abstract:
How does fiscal stimulus affect durable goods sales and to what extent does stimulus drive inflation? We study this question in the context of how the unprecedented pandemic fiscal stimulus affected household car purchases and auto prices. Using administrative data on vehicle registrations, we exploit the timing of nearly $900 billion in stimulus payments and geographic differences in program exposure to identify causal effects on sales. We find the stimulus increased purchases by 5.5 million vehicles (3.2%) during 2020–2022, implying a medium-run (3-year) marginal propensity to spend (MPX) on autos of 0.19 and a total marginal propensity to consume (MPC) of 0.47. Despite this substantial demand response, fiscal transfers account for less than 20% of the surge in auto prices. In a general equilibrium model with new and used markets, we show how secondary-market interactions dampen inflation. When transfers push households onto the new-car margin, trade-ins expand used supply and limit price increases. This channel weakens when supply is tight or when policy targets borrowing constraints, in which case stimulus manifests more as inflation than output. Non-fiscal factors, including supply constraints, relaxed credit conditions, and preference shifts, explain the majority of the observed inflation.

title: Physician Competition: Entry and Substitution

detail.title: Physician Competition: Entry and Substitution
detail.abstract:
We describe competition in the physician market, focusing on how entry barriers and substitution possibilities have changed in recent decades. Regulatory caps on medical school seats and residency slots—especially for high-paying specialties—continue to ration entry, generate high returns for those who gain these slots, and direct the most academically accomplished trainees toward lucrative fields. But trained physicians increasingly compete with nurse practitioners, physician assistants, and other mid-level practitioners in the market for patients. Training of these substitutes has expanded far more rapidly than physician supply. We present key facts about the physician pipeline, a conceptual framework linking specialty earnings to entry barriers, and describe the rise of mid-level providers. These facts mean that effective competition policy in physician markets must look beyond conventional concentration measures and focus on the institutions and laws that govern who can provide medical care.

We compare physician incomes using tax data from the United States, Canada, Sweden, and the Netherlands. Physicians are concentrated in the top percentiles of the income distribution in all four countries, especially in the United States and certain specialties. Physician incomes are highest in the United States, and a decomposition shows that this mainly reflects differences in overall income distributions, rather than physicians’ locations in those distributions. This suggests that broader labor market differences, and thus physicians’ outside options, drive absolute incomes. Shifting US physicians’ incomes to match relative positions in other countries’ distributions would only marginally reduce healthcare spending.

detail.abstract: This study examines the relation between blockchain adoption and investment efficiency. Using a difference-in-differences approach with a matched sample of firms that disclosed blockchain adoption in 8-K filings between 2014 and 2023, we find that adopters exhibit higher investment efficiency after adoption compared to non-adopters. We also find that blockchain adoption is positively associated with financial reporting quality, suggesting that enhanced financial reporting quality might be a mechanism through which blockchain adoption improves investment efficiency. Further analyses show that the effect of blockchain adoption on investment efficiency varies with firms’ information environments and across types of blockchain applications. The effect is most pronounced among firms with weak information environments and those adopting non-cryptocurrency applications, where blockchain’s potential to improve investment efficiency is expected to be greater. Overall, our findings provide insights into how blockchain technology can influence financial reporting practices and corporate investment decisions.

detail.abstract: Artificial intelligence systems are now embedded across defense infrastructure, financial markets, healthcare systems, and intimate human-computer interfaces. While innovation has accelerated, governance sequencing has lagged. This paper revisits and reformulates a constitutional framework for AI governance originally articulated in 2000-2001, integrating contemporary Human-Computer Interaction research, relational AI attachment dynamics, environmental externalities, and economic concentration risk. The central argument is that governance must precede irreversible deployment. As AI systems increasingly simulate agency, influence military decision cycles, and concentrate structural power, regulatory architecture must safeguard human dignity, ecological stability, and democratic continuity. Artificial intelligence may evolve; human sovereignty must remain paramount. I. The Sequencing Problem: Governance Before Launch Technological history demonstrates that large-scale deployment often precedes regulatory maturity. Artificial intelligence represents a consequential inflection point due to its integration across military systems, financial markets, healthcare infrastructure, information ecosystems, and emotional interfaces. Once embedded at scale, rollback becomes improbable. Governance must therefore precede deployment in critical domains.

title: Blockchain Technology for Traditional Finance
affiliations: University of Chicago - Booth School of Business and Harvard University

detail.title: Blockchain Technology for Traditional Finance
detail.abstract:
Blockchain technology as embodied in cryptocurrencies like Bitcoin and Ethereum is comprised of both (a) a novel data structure and (b) a novel trust model. This paper analyzes the potential gains for traditional finance from an idealized version of the novel data structure on its own, with trust instead anchored in traditional sources such as rule of law, reputations, relationships, and collateral. Our framework has two parts. First, we analyze potential improvements for financial transactions that are already taking place. We identify three categories of improvement: (i) reducing real resource costs, (ii) improving balance sheet efficiency, and (iii) reducing intermediation rents. While the value of such improvements is hard to quantify precisely, we estimate that potential gains could be significant, especially the reduction in rents. Second, we analyze the potential for the technology to facilitate new transactions. We identify three channels: (i) making it more technologically difficult to cheat, (ii) making it easier to punish a cheating counterparty in a static sense, and (iii) making it easier to punish a cheating counterparty in a dynamic sense. Our key insight is that the potential gains are large if and only if there is a long tail of relatively low surplus, relatively infrequent transactions for which traditional forms of trust are insufficient. Last, we apply our framework to stablecoins. We conclude that if there are large gains from stablecoins for legal actors they are most likely to come from stablecoins putting pressure on intermediation rents or inefficient regulation, or from the programmability of stablecoins facilitating a large number of small transactions that otherwise would not have been trustworthy.

title: Payment Fraud and Welfare

detail.title: Payment Fraud and Welfare
detail.abstract: This paper studies the welfare consequences of imperfect payment recognizability in a monetary search model. Sellers observe a noisy signal of payment authenticity and choose acceptance thresholds that balance fraud losses against the rejection of legitimate payments. The information structure maps directly to the ROC--AUC statistic used to evaluate fraud detection systems, linking modern payment technology to monetary theory. Calibrating the model to e-commerce payment fraud statistics, seller profit margins, and money demand, I find that perfect recognizability increases online trading volume by about 10\%, raises seller profits by 27\%, and improves gains from trade in the decentralized market by about 2\%. Moreover, introducing a competing payment instrument with 10\% higher recognizability, and allowing sellers to choose which payment to accept, leads to sizable adoption: the new instrument captures 5--16\% of online transactions even when its yield is 25--100 basis points below that of bank deposits.

title: Busing & The Sanctuary City
affiliations: University of Colorado at Boulder - University of Colorado Law School, Rutgers Law School and University of North Carolina School of Law

detail.title: Busing & The Sanctuary City
detail.abstract: Sanctuary cities demonstrated notable legal resilience during the first Trump administration, withstanding legal and political pressure aimed at dismantling their policies. That resilience, however, was undermined by Texas's busing program in 2022 and 2023 in ways that earlier legal and political attacks could not achieve. As this Article argues, busing succeeded not merely by imposing fiscal and logistical burdens, but by surfacing longstanding internal cleavages and ultimately fracturing the coalition that sustained the sanctuary movement. This Article advances a theoretical framework that understands sanctuary cities not as a uniform policy, but as a coalition-based form of local governance, composed of distinct and sometimes conflicting commitments. Within this framework, we identify three distinct strands within the sanctuary movement-administrative sanctuaries, political sanctuaries, and welcoming cities-each of which pulled sanctuary policies toward dissimilar interests. While the unification of these strands under a single policy umbrella drove the movement's initial rise, the busing crisis did more than merely reveal these dividing lines; it exploited them to devastating effect. Through comparative case studies of New York, Chicago, and Denver, this Article provides empirical evidence of how migrant busing fractured the legal and administrative coalitions underlying sanctuary governance. By theorizing the connections between busing and sanctuary cities offers not only a new theoretical framework but also a warning: without reckoning with its internal divisions, the sanctuary movement may prove far more fragile than its legal victories suggest.

title: School Choice and Segregation: Evidence from the Oakland Unified School District

detail.title: School Choice and Segregation: Evidence from the Oakland Unified School District
detail.abstract:
We study the prospects for changes in school priorities to reduce income segregation in a context of centralized school assignment, accounting for behavioral responses to school offers. Promoting integration is a central objective for large urban school districts in the US, and reforms to school assignment priorities are a prominent means of pursuing this goal. Such efforts may be constrained by students' decisions to exit the public school system in response to less-preferred school offers. Using data on kindergarten applicants to the Oakland Unified School District (OUSD), we show that offers of spots at first-choice schools boost the likelihood that applicants remain in OUSD. Nevertheless, simulations show that policy reforms giving priority for low-income students at high-income schools can substantially reduce segregation with minimal impacts on retention in the district.

title: max EPS Payout Policy
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) and Michigan State University - Eli Broad College of Business

detail.title: max EPS Payout Policy
detail.abstract:
Holding cash has a cost. For an EPS-maximizing CEO, that cost equals her firm’s earnings yield. EPS maximizers retain cash when they can get an even higher yield by investing the money. Otherwise, they return cash to shareholders. This is the EPS-maximizing payout policy. Growth stocks (EY < rf) never return cash because they can clear their low earnings-yield hurdle by investing in risk-free bonds. Value stocks (EY > rf) face a higher hurdle, which makes cash their cheapest source of capital but also raises the opportunity cost of retention. Value stocks return cash when they cannot invest in enough high-yield projects to make up for the higher cost. Paradoxically, the firms that are most likely to distribute cash—deep value stocks (EY ≫ rf)—are also the ones for whom internal cash is cheapest relative to external financing. Dividends and buybacks both deliver the same value to shareholders, but only buybacks can be accretive. Hence, EPS-maximizing CEOs prefer to distribute via buybacks. Some firms pay dividends for reasons outside our model. Such departures should concentrate among marginal value stocks (EY ≈ rf + ε) where the accretive pull of buybacks is weakest. Empirically, this logic explains which firms return cash, how they distribute the money, and time-series trends.

title: The Emergence of Regional Cultures in the United States

detail.title: The Emergence of Regional Cultures in the United States
detail.abstract:
This paper recovers the cultural geography of the United States from first-name patterns in census data spanning 1850 to 1930. Using unsupervised clustering of county-level name distributions, we identify spatially coherent cultural regions that align with historically recognized settlement patterns and remain stable across eight decades of economic and institutional change. The deepest division separates North from South, but finer groupings (New England, the Mid-Atlantic, Appalachia, the Deep South) emerge as nested subregions. Formal tests confirm that the recovered clusters are spatially contiguous, temporally persistent, and robust to resampling. The findings bear on whether liberal institutions require cultural homogeneity, whether cultural pluralism is a source of resilience or fragility, and how the imprint of early settlement shapes the practice of self-governance.

detail.title: Heterogeneous Wage Gaps in Korea's Dual Labor Market
detail.abstract: Labor market duality in South Korea is widely regarded as a key driver of wage inequality. Using nationally representative panel data, this paper estimates wage differentials between regular and non-regular workers within fixed effects and correlated random effects (CRE) frameworks to address unobserved heterogeneity correlated with employment status. We examine both average and distributional wage gaps. We find that substantial wage penalties for non-regular workers persist even after controlling for observed characteristics and individual fixed effects. The distributional analysis reveals pronounced heterogeneity across the wage distribution, indicating that employment duality contributes to inequality beyond mean differences. A detailed heterogeneity analysis indicates that occupational composition plays a key role in explaining these differentials. These findings imply that policies targeting employment status alone may be insufficient to reduce wage inequality and highlight the broader relevance of dual labor market structures.

title: Artificial Intelligence and the Gender Wage Gap: Two Competing Mechanisms

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and the Gender Wage Gap: Two Competing Mechanisms
detail.abstract: Does artificial intelligence narrow or widen the gender wage gap? I document that AI has two competing effects whose relative strength determines the answer. Crosssectionally, occupations with high AI exposure exhibit gender wage gaps five times smaller than low-exposure occupations (6% vs. 29%), a pattern driven by the objective measurability of output in AI-intensive jobs. However, exploiting time-varying industry-level AI adoption from Babina et al. (2024)-instrumented with university AI talent supply shocks-I find that industries which adopted more AI saw wider gender wage gaps, consistent with men adopting AI tools more aggressively than women. To disentangle these forces, I develop a structural employer learning model where AI improves the precision of productivity signals. The model reveals that women face 39% noisier baseline signals, and that AI could reduce the gender wage gap by 62% through improved signal precision-but only if women gain equal access to AI tools. Combining AI adoption with policies that reduce career interruptions (e.g., universal childcare).

title: Zombies, AI, and the "Objective" Theory of Contracts
affiliations: University of Iowa - College of Law

detail.title: Zombies, AI, and the "Objective" Theory of Contracts
detail.abstract: “Agentic” “AI” that can pass the “Turing Test” might behave in ways externally indistinguishable from persons but without our subjectivity or mental states. Under the so-called “objective” theory of contracts, taught as black letter in the common law world for a century, this is purportedly enough for large language models to enter into self-binding contracts. In contrast, this Chapter argues that this possibility offers a reductio in favor the alternative view that takes the “objective” theory as the law’s evidentiary commitment rather than a normative or metaphysical one. For starters, it is not clear that language “agreed upon” by entities without mental states means anything, at least not anything anyone cares about. More generally, there is no normative reason for the law to attempt to enforce the output of probabilistic language models entirely disconnected from subjective intent; the only possible justifications of contract are, in the end, “subjectivist.”

detail.abstract: We introduce an econometric model in which the conditional mean and variance have long memory with dynamic degrees of fractional integration. The model is named the `score-driven fractionally integrated quasi-autoregressive (QAR) and fractionally integrated Beta-t-EGARCH (exponential generalized autoregressive conditional heteroscedasticity) model with Student's t innovations’, FI(d_mu,t)-t-QAR-FI(d_lambda,t)-Beta-$-EGARCH. In this model, (i) the mean return (mu_t), (ii) the degree of fractional integration of mean return (d_mu,t), (iii) the log scale of return (lambda_t), and (iv) the degree of fractional integration of the log scale of return (d_lambda,t) are four score-driven filters. We compare the in-sample and out-of-sample performances of FI(d_mu,t)-t-QAR-FI(d_lambda,t)-Beta-t-EGARCH with several score-driven models (e.g. Beta-t-EGARCH), t-GARCH, and ARMA-t-GARCH (AR moving average, ARMA). We use daily data of the NIFTY-50 and SENSEX indices from the Indian stock market. The in-sample period is from July 3, 1990, to April 24, 2025. The out-of-sample volatility forecasting period is the COVID-19 (coronavirus disease of 2019) pandemic from March 2, 2020, to May 31, 2023. We find that FI(d_mu,t)-$t$-QAR-FI (d_lambda,t)-Beta-t-EGARCH improves in-sample and out-of-sample performance relative to other models, indicating for investors that it is an efficient alternative to benchmark classical and score-driven I(0) models of mean return and volatility.

title:
What Do Treatment Effects Measure? 
Marginal Responses and Financial Constraints in Corporate Finance

detail.title:
What Do Treatment Effects Measure? 
Marginal Responses and Financial Constraints in Corporate Finance
detail.abstract: Three prominent studies (Rauh, 2006; Lemmon and Roberts, 2010; Bakke and Whited, 2012) all estimate the causal effect of financing on investment. They find sharply different values of zero, 0.65, and one. This paper explains why all three are correct. In a canonical investment model, the marginal response of investment to financing is binary. It is one for constrained firms, zero for unconstrained firms. The local average treatment effect recovers the share of constrained firms among compliers. It is not a structural elasticity. Those three studies all estimate the same structural relationship. What differs is the respective sets of complier firms. Evidence from the broader quasi-experimental literature confirms the pattern. Estimates approach zero for unconstrained subsamples and one for constrained subsamples. An intermediate treatment effect is not a structural parameter. It is evidence of population heterogeneity. Generalizing estimates across settings requires explicit accounting for constraint shares. This paper also develops diagnostics distinguishing the binary specification from smooth alternatives and examines extensions for large shocks and precautionary savings.

detail.abstract: We study how career incentives in the public sector affect government officials’ stress and health, using visible aging as a scalable proxy. Using administrative health inspection data, we show that the difference between individuals’ apparent age and chronological age is a strong predictor of subsequent health outcomes.. We then construct a panel of mayors and senior officials and apply computer-vision models to estimate apparent age from official photographs. Officials in jurisdictions with weaker economic performance age significantly faster. Linking outcomes to promotion incentives, we show that the effect concentrates where promotion tournaments are steeper and downside risk is greater, consistent with both rewards and punishments shaping stress exposure. To corroborate the mechanism, we use large language models to analyze officials’ speeches and government reports, extracting measures of urgency, constraint, and risk emphasis that rise when officials age faster and predict within-official changes in apparent age. Together, AI-based facial and textual measures reveal substantial human-capital costs of promotion pressure in public office.

detail.abstract: A central explanation for domestic audience costs---the decrease in approval leaders face when backing down from a previous threat---is that domestic audiences seek to avoid the international repercussions of failing to honor their country's commitments. But how do international audiences actually react to foreign leaders' actions during crises? We develop a theory of allied audience costs, specifying how and why foreign publics within allied states respond when leaders make threats they fail to carry out. First, we argue that allied audiences, like their domestic counterparts, impose "inconsistency costs" on leaders who say one thing and do another. Second, because many allied citizens prefer to deter common adversaries, they reward leaders who issue threats that signal aggressive behavior. This "belligerence benefit" contrasts with domestic audience cost theories that emphasize penalties for belligerence. Third, the magnitude of this benefit depends on individual beliefs, such as concerns of entrapment and abandonment. Evidence from a survey experiment in Japan supports these expectations. These findings show that allied audiences evaluate leaders using logics that differ from those operating within domestic publics, creating distinct incentives during military crises.

title: Bubble Mitigation Policies: Counterfactual Analysis and Treatment Effect Inference

detail.title: Bubble Mitigation Policies: Counterfactual Analysis and Treatment Effect Inference
detail.abstract: To safeguard economic and financial stability policymakers regularly take actions designed to increase resilience to systemic risks and curb speculative market behavior. To assess the effectiveness of such mitigation policies, we introduce a counterfactual approach tailored to accommodate the mildly explosive dynamics that occur during speculative bubbles. We derive asymptotics of the estimated treatment effect under a common factor structure that allows for explosive, I(1), and stationary factors, thereby having applicability to a wide range of prevailing economic conditions. An inferential procedure is proposed for the policy treatment effect that has asymptotic validity and demonstrates satisfactory finite sample performance. An empirical analysis examines the monetary policy of interest rate hikes implemented by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, beginning in October 2021. This policy is shown to have exerted a delayed and regionally heterogeneous cooling effect on New Zealand housing markets. While short run impacts are limited, a longer post-treatment window reveals evidence of monetary policy transmission, with house prices clearly declining relative to their counterfactual paths in some regions.

title: Navigating Expertise in Adjudication

detail.title: Navigating Expertise in Adjudication
detail.abstract:
Modern adjudication is increasingly defined by its encounter with expert testimony. From toxic torts to data science, trials now depend on forms of specialized knowledge that lie far beyond the ordinary competence of lay decisionmakers. This dependence gives rise to a persistent epistemic dilemma: whether the law should attempt to educate factfinders to evaluate expert claims for themselves, or instead direct them to defer to expert authority. Each response is unsatisfying. Education preserves the ideal of autonomous judgment but strains against severe limits of time, resources, and cognition in the courtroom. Deference accommodates specialization but risks insulating expertise from meaningful contestation and transforming adjudication into a ritual of authority rather than a forum of reasoned proof.

This Article argues that the education–deference binary mislocates the problem. The epistemic legitimacy of adjudication turns not only on evidentiary standards, but on institutional design. Rather than oscillating between pedagogical ambition and technocratic concession, courts can pursue structural arrangements that reshape how expertise is introduced, tested, and translated into legal judgment. Examining a range of institutional alternatives—from neutral and jointly retained experts to specialized adjudicators and redesigned modes of adversarial engagement—the Article shows how different architectures of factfinding redistribute epistemic authority and risk.

The stakes are institutional and constitutional. A legal system that cannot integrate expert knowledge while preserving transparency, contestation, and intelligibility risks eroding the trial’s claim to democratic legitimacy. But a system that adapts its structures to accommodate expertise without surrender can preserve the trial’s core commitment to reasoned judgment even under conditions of deep specialization. The problem of expertise, in short, is not merely doctrinal. It is structural, and the future of adjudication depends on how law designs the institutions through which expert knowledge is made legally intelligible.

title: Artificial Intelligence and Environmental, Social, and Governance: A Hybrid Bibliometric Approach

detail.abstract: This study provides a comprehensive overview of research on artificial intelligence (AI) and Environmental, Social, and Governance (ESG) by creating a knowledge map of the field. Using a systematic-bibliometric approach, we quantitatively analyzed a total of 129 documents, which collectively were cited 4276 times (2017-2024). Following performance analysis, we conducted a rigorous systematic literature review, critically evaluating each document to identify key research methods, geographic focus, theories, and frameworks. We then performed citation network and co-citation analyses to uncover the intellectual foundations of the field. We also employed bibliographic coupling to identify emerging research streams, while thematic evaluation provided insights into the evolution of research areas over time, highlighting both the most and least explored themes. Finally, our complementary systematic-bibliometric analyses enabled us to derive an integrated framework outlining key antecedents, mediators, moderators, and outcomes. This in turn allows us to develop a structured conclusion for each of the six identified research clusters, which will guide future research directions in AI and ESG. We also discuss practical and theoretical implications, offering valuable insights for scholars and practitioners in the field.

title: Two-Time-Scale Transfer Learning for Market-by-Order Micro-Return Forecasting
affiliations: University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB), University of California Santa Barbara and University of California, Santa Barbara (UCSB)

detail.title: Two-Time-Scale Transfer Learning for Market-by-Order Micro-Return Forecasting

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: Deep Learning models face a critical "simulation-to-reality" gap when applied to high-frequency financial data. Deep learning models often fail to capture the non-stationary dynamics of live markets requiring computationally expensive recalibrations. This work introduces the Two-TimeScale Transfer Learning (TTSTL) framework, a hybrid model architecture that combines the flexibility of deep learning models with the parsimony and calibration ease of time series regression models. The TTSTL architecture mimics the hippocampus-neocortex interaction in the human brain by coupling a high-capacity deep learning "backbone" with a lightweight, adaptive time series regression "adapter." The backbone, utilizing a Convolutional Neural Network-Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) network, extracts complex, non-linear feature interactions from event-driven Limit Order Book (LOB) data, while the adapter-implemented as a Hybrid Autoregressive Moving Average with Exogenous variables-Generalized Autoregressive Conditional Heteroskedasticity (ARMAX-GARCH)-DeepLOB model-integrates these features into a statistical framework for micro-return forecasting. Experiments are conducted on synthetic and Intel (INTC) Market-by-Order (MBO) data. Results demonstrate that the TTSTL framework significantly outperforms standalone deep learning baselines in terms of accuracy (RelMAE), while also enabling volatility modeling and probabilistic forecasting.

title: Demand Drivers of Central Bank Liquidity: A Time-to-Exit TLTRO Analysis
affiliations: European Central Bank (ECB) and Banco de España

detail.title: Demand Drivers of Central Bank Liquidity: A Time-to-Exit TLTRO Analysis

publicationDetails.detailsText: Banco de Espana Working Paper No. 2548
publicationDetails.journalName: Banco de Espana Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: We exploit banks’ early repayments of targeted longer-term refinancing operations (TLTRO) following the program’s recalibration in October 2022 as a laboratory to uncover demand drivers of central bank liquidity. We formulate and estimate a discrete-time hazard model to early exit from TLTRO to identify what bank (country) characteristics drive a sticky, prolonged demand for central bank (long-term) operations as opposed to an early exit from such facilities. We also examine whether the more liquidity-risk exposed banks during the TLTRO phasing out period had a higher probability of becoming “liquidity dependent” on the ECB when exiting (Acharya et al., 2023). Finally, we discuss the policy implications of our findings, particularly in the context of the recent review of the ECB’s operational framework.

title: HIV Service Delivery Disruptions Following the PEPFAR and USAID HIV Funding Withdrawal in Uganda and Zimbabwe: An Interrupted Time-Series Study

detail.title: HIV Service Delivery Disruptions Following the PEPFAR and USAID HIV Funding Withdrawal in Uganda and Zimbabwe: An Interrupted Time-Series Study

declarations.declarationOfInterest: Contributing organisations received US Government HIV funding prior to January 2025 that was subsequently terminated. Identities of organisations are withheld to prevent potential future funding repercussions.
declarations.funderStatement: Funding for this study was provided by The Josiah Charles Trent Memorial Foundation Endowment Fund at Duke University.

detail.abstract:
Background: In January 2025, the US government froze foreign aid and dismantled USAID, abruptly halting PEPFAR, the largest external funder of HIV services globally. A narrow humanitarian waiver preserved ‘lifesaving’ services, but prevention, testing, and treatment programmes were severely impacted, particularly for key-populations. Quantitative evidence of real-world impacts on non-governmental organisations (NGOs) that directly lost funding has been absent. We aimed to estimate the effect of the funding cuts on HIV service delivery across prevention, testing, and treatment in Uganda and Zimbabwe.

Methods: In this interrupted time-series study, we used monthly and quarterly service-delivery data from four NGOs in Uganda and Zimbabwe, all of which received stop-work orders and did not have US funding reinstated. Core service indicators across prevention, treatment, and testing domains were normalised into indices where 100 represents their average 2024 level. We applied segmented regression specifying February 2025 as the interruption point; each index point approximates the percentage difference from the 2024 average.

Findings: All three service domains showed large, immediate, and sustained declines. Prevention services fell by 55–64 index points, testing by 50–53 index points, and treatment by 29 index points relative to 2024 average levels (all p<0·001). The ART humanitarian waiver attenuated treatment impacts but did not prevent substantial decline.

Interpretation: The sudden withdrawal of US funding produced severe, sustained disruptions to HIV service delivery in Uganda and Zimbabwe, with prevention and testing most acutely affected. These are the first quantitative findings from organisations whose US funding was terminated and apply to a significant portion of HIV services in high-prevalence settings, particularly for key populations. Estimates likely understate broader national impacts due to organisational survivor bias and health service delivery mix. Urgent investment in service-continuity, transition funding, and long-term domestic financing strategies is needed to prevent infection rebounds.​
