title: Why Was India Able To Beat Britain At Jute But Not At Cotton Textile Manufacturing?

detail.title: Why Was India Able To Beat Britain At Jute But Not At Cotton Textile Manufacturing?
detail.abstract: This paper undertakes a detailed productivity and competitiveness comparison for the cotton and jute textile industries in Britain and India for the period 1860-1940 to examine why India was only able to beat Britain decisively in jute but not cotton. I collect data on factor costs over the period, and examine differences in capital productivity rates. I assess the extent to which manning ratios differed between the two countries for the two industries and whether they changed over time. I then construct implied unit cost ratios, with and without allowing for capital-labour substitution, and use these to infer productivity differences. As the UK had far higher wages but only marginally lower capital costs for the vast majority of the period, India should have had an absolute cost advantage in both industries, even at British factor proportions, that could only have been increased by capital-labour substitution. This implies some missing (labour) productivity residual in the UK's favour, at least for cotton. I examine an old and hotly debated hypothesis that differences in labour intensity per worker (assuming manning ratios reflected this) explain this productivity gap, while explicitly allowing capital-labour substitution. Observed differences in manning ratios quantitatively explain the majority of the required productivity gap for cotton, but not jute, throughout the period, and my implied potential increases in profits for Indian firms that reduced manning rates are large and persistent enough to rule out managerial failures (the alternative hypothesis in the literature) as their cause. Such labour intensity differences per worker between the UK and India, relative to the wage ratio, were smaller for jute than for cotton, which explains why India was relatively successful in that industry, and Britain in the other.

title: The Causal Effect of Happiness and Fear on Test Scores
affiliations: University of Arizona,  University of Arizona - Department of Agricultural and Resource Economics and The University of Arizona

detail.title: The Causal Effect of Happiness and Fear on Test Scores
detail.abstract: While emotional states are widely correlated with academic performance, causal evidence remains limited. We investigate the causal effect of incidental emotions on verbal test performance using a laboratory experiment with undergraduate students. Participants were randomly assigned to either a Fear, Happiness, or Neutral condition induced through immersive virtual-reality videos immediately prior to completing a timed SAT-style verbal test. While the Happiness manipulation did not significantly alter emotional state, Fear was successfully induced. Fear induction increased verbal test scores overall, with effects concentrated among non-native English speakers and male participants. We do not observe performance gains for native speakers or female participants despite successful Fear induction within these groups. Personality traits do not predict test scores. These findings contrast with prior evidence from an SAT-style mathematics test, suggesting that emotions interact with academic performance in domain-specific ways. Moreover, it appears that emotional effects differ sharply between advantaged and disadvantaged test takers, which highlights the importance of context and heterogeneity in understanding the psychology of academic performance.

title: Energy and Transport poverty in the European Union and UK: A bibliometric and systematic literature analysis
affiliations: IMT Institute for Advanced Studies, IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca and IMT School for Advanced Studies Lucca

detail.title: Energy and Transport poverty in the European Union and UK: A bibliometric and systematic literature analysis
detail.abstract: In the present study we map the intellectual structure of research on energy poverty andtransport poverty in the European Union and the United Kingdom, with the goal of betterdefine the theoretical perimeter of the field and identify major debates. The analysis coverscore publications from 2011–2024 and applies established bibliometric and systematicreview protocols, implemented through Bibliometrix and VOSviewer to ensuretransparency and reproducibility.Bibliographic coupling identifies five clusters in the energy poverty literature and four in thetransport poverty literature, all with a pronounced multidisciplinary orientation. Studies thataddress energy poverty and transport poverty jointly tend to lie at the margins of theseclusters, indicating the novelty of this combined perspective. A systematic review of theclustered publications then delineates the theoretical boundaries of the field and identifieskey debates, methodological approaches, and emerging policy implications concerningenergy poverty, transport poverty, and their intersection as Double Energy Vulnerability.Building on this, we propose an interpretative framework that connects the clustersthrough themes such as local policy design and territorial context. Drawing on place-basedtheories and policy frameworks, we refine this categorisation and orient future research onDouble Energy Vulnerability and the role of local policies.

title: Crouching energy poverty, hidden heating costs: Applying energy poverty measurement in a Nordic country
affiliations: , Government of the Republic of Finland - Finnish Environment Institute and Government of the Republic of Finland - Finnish Environment Institute

detail.title: Crouching energy poverty, hidden heating costs: Applying energy poverty measurement in a Nordic country
detail.abstract: A Nordic geographical location and electricity price volatility are obvious risk factors for energy poverty among impoverished households. Still, governmental policies have not specifically targeted its causes and consequences. In this article, we bring a lacking Nordic perspective on expenditure-based energy poverty measurement. We utilise the Household Budget Survey database for Finland, which we complement with relevant national housing, energy cost and building datasets and modelled hidden heating costs in warm-rent arrangements. Our results show that the share of households with energy poverty in Finland varied in 2022: 14.8% (for the twice-the-median indicator), 9.9% (for the cost-burden indicator), 9.1% (for the low-income high-cost indicator LIHC), 8.1% (for the low-income low energy efficiency indicator) and 6.9% (for a novel combination indicator). Our corrective modelling proves significant over-statement of energy poverty according to expenditure-median based indicators in European databases. We show that low-income electricity and oil-heated households situated in non-urban areas have a higher probability of suffering from energy poverty. Wood heating gives a more nuanced picture. On one hand, using wood heating as the main heating source increases the probability of being energy-poor (for the LIHC indicator), but it generally decreases the cost burden of the population due to its broad utilization as ancillary heating. To date, this is the first expenditure-based energy poverty study from Nordic countries that is based on nationally representative cross-sectional household microdata.

title: Revealing Tax Evasion: Experimental Evidence from a Representative Survey of Indonesian Firms
affiliations: World Bank,  and World Bank

detail.title: Revealing Tax Evasion: Experimental Evidence from a Representative Survey of Indonesian Firms

declarations.funderStatement: The work was made possible by funding support from European Union, SECO and Canada under Indonesia PFM MDTF Phase III Program, together with funding from the World Bank Global Tax Program and the Gates Foundation.

detail.abstract: Measuring tax evasion by firms is notoriously difficult: direct questions yield biased responses while administrative data captures only detected violations. This paper examines the pervasiveness of tax evasion in Indonesia and the characteristics associated with non-compliance through a randomized, double-list experiment embedded in a nationally representative survey of 2,955 registered firms that preserves anonymity. The results reveal that around a quarter of firms indirectly admit to evading tax, which is equivalent to a revenue loss of two percent of GDP.  Firms that do not export, face informal sector competition, and believe tax administration is a major obstacle are the most likely to evade taxes. These findings help inform tax authorities, which face substantial challenges in estimating levels of tax evasion and identifying non-compliant taxpayers. This study provides the first validation that double-list experiments reliably measure sensitive organizational behaviors and offers representative estimates of firm tax evasion in a major middle-income country.

title: The Policy Put: Option-Implied Disaster Risk and Macroeconomic Dynamics in China
affiliations: Shanghai University of International Business and Economics and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: The Policy Put: Option-Implied Disaster Risk and Macroeconomic Dynamics in China
detail.abstract: We extract a time-varying physical disaster probability (ˆpt) from deep out-of-themoney put options on the SSE 50 ETF (2015–2024) in China. Consistent with rare-disaster theory, ˆpt strongly captures contemporaneous downside economic conditions. However, we document a “Predictive Disconnect”: option-implied disaster probability exhibits negligible predictive power for subsequent GDP growth, challenging the baseline prediction that higher disaster risk should depress future output. We argue that this disconnect reflects a “Macroeconomic Policy Put”. Surges in ˆpt act as tripwires in the government’s reaction function, triggering countercyclical fiscal and monetary expansions that truncate the left tail of the future growth distribution. Priced disaster risk thus reflects pre-intervention fundamentals, whereas realized macroeconomic outcomes reflect post-intervention equilibria.

title: How Crowdfunding Shapes Young Innovative Venture Financing
affiliations: MBS School of Business and Aix-Marseille University

detail.title: How Crowdfunding Shapes Young Innovative Venture Financing
detail.abstract: Crowdfunding is a digital alternative to traditional early-stage financing, competing with business angels and venture capitalists. Entrepreneurs must decide not only which source of external finance to pursue but also in what sequence. We develop a theoretical framework to analyze this choice in a two-stage setting with investor competition. Depending on transaction costs, support quality, monitoring efficiency, and valuation parameters, either traditional investors or the crowd may hold a competitive advantage. The model characterizes the entrepreneur’s optimal funding source and predicts rational financing sequences as well as differences between ventures backed by traditional investors and those financed through crowdfunding. The results highlight how the availability of crowdfunding expands entrepreneurs’ outside options, shifts bargaining power, and generates substitution effects that require traditional early-stage investors to strengthen their expertise and specialization to remain competitive.

title: Stress Tests on Main Street: Tracing Holding-Company Exposure through Branch Networks

detail.title: Stress Tests on Main Street: Tracing Holding-Company Exposure through Branch Networks
detail.abstract: The most consequential critique of post-crisis stress testing, that supervisory capital constraints   depress credit supply and local growth, is not supported by the data. I evaluate   this growth-penalty hypothesis using U.S. CCAR and a county-level exposure measure   that traces holding-company regulation through subsidiary ownership chains and branch   deposit networks, where cross-county variation is largely predetermined by slow-moving   banking geography rather than local conditions. Local projections consistently reject   the hypothesis: cumulative income responses are positive, concentrated in proprietor   and capital-type income, and robust across stress-test regimes and exposure definitions.   Stress-tested banks raised capital and reduced wholesale funding without contracting   lending — balance-sheet strengthening rather than credit retrenchment.

title: Unlocking Trade Credit Dynamics: How U.S. Monetary Policy Impacts Emerging Markets' Supply Chains
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and Central University of Finance and Economics (CUFE)

detail.title: Unlocking Trade Credit Dynamics: How U.S. Monetary Policy Impacts Emerging Markets' Supply Chains
detail.abstract: Using firm-level data from 15 emerging market economies (EMEs) between 2003Q1 and 2021Q4, we analyze the impact of U.S. monetary policy on trade credit provided by suppliers that issue foreign currency bonds. Our findings reveal that during periods of U.S. monetary policy easing, these suppliers increase trade credit to customers that do not issue foreign currency bonds, alleviating the latter’s financing constraints and facilitating sales. Notably, this effect is asymmetric, as suppliers maintain trade credit during U.S. monetary tightening due to the stability of supplier-customer relationships. Our results suggest that during U.S. monetary easing, EMEs should adopt floating exchange rate regimes and capital controls to mitigate the associated effects. Conversely, during tightening, floating exchange rates can help absorb external shocks. Our study provides micro-level evidence that supports the “2.5-lemma” paradox.

title: Pricing Kernel (Non)Monotonicity and Conditional Information
affiliations: National University of Singapore (NUS), Business School, Sun Yat-Sen University, Blockchain Research Center Humboldt-Universität zu Berlin, Humboldt-University of Berlin and National University of Singapore (NUS)

detail.title: Pricing Kernel (Non)Monotonicity and Conditional Information
detail.abstract: Estimation of pricing kernels has attracted substantial attention following the emergence of the "pricing kernel (PK) puzzle". When the physical density is estimated from historical market returns while the risk-neutral density is derived from option prices with forward-looking information set, one often obtains a non-monotonic PK slope. The Conditional Density Integration (CDI) estimator seeks to address this mismatch by incorporating option-implied forward-looking information to recover theory-consistent kernels. However, we find that CDI does not completely resolve the puzzle; relative to traditional methods, it can still generate non-monotonic kernels that contradict the standard expected-utility theory for risk-averse investors. Moreover, monotonicity depends critically on assumptions of constant market volatility and is highly sensitive to smoothing parameters. Evidence from S&P 500 and Bitcoin options confirms that volatility jumps undermine monotonicity. Our findings highlight fragility and stability challenges in pricing kernel estimation.

title: The Billion-Naira Benchmark: Navigating the Sec 2026 Recapitalization Era
affiliations: University of Nigeria

detail.title: The Billion-Naira Benchmark: Navigating the Sec 2026 Recapitalization Era
detail.abstract: The Nigerian capital market is currently undergoing its most significant structural transformation in over a decade. On January 16, 2026, the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) issued Circular Number 26-1, titled "Revised Minimum Capital (MC) for Regulated Capital Market Entities." This directive is not merely an administrative adjustment; it is a profound regulatory intervention designed to insulate the financial ecosystem from systemic collapse and to align with the Federal Government's vision of a $1 Trillion Economy by 2030. As we examine this policy, we must look beyond the staggering percentages and explore the statutory foundations, the socioeconomic necessity, and the strategies available to Capital Market Operators (CMOs).

title: Debt overhang and intangible investment: The moderating role of ESG performance
affiliations: , University of Ljubljana School of Economics and Business and University of Ljubljana - Faculty of Economics

detail.title: Debt overhang and intangible investment: The moderating role of ESG performance
detail.abstract: We examine the relationship between firm intangible investment, leverage, and ESG performance. Using an unbalanced panel of 1,824 publicly listed US firms from 2015 to 2023, we find a strong negative relationship between intangible investment and leverage, consistent with the debt overhang hypothesis. Importantly, we show that strong ESG performance significantly mitigates this negative relationship. The moderating effect of ESG is particularly pronounced for intangible rather than physical investment. We propose three pillar-specific economic channels through which ESG moderates investment constraints: the environmental risk channel, the social capital channel, and the agency channel. The moderating role is driven primarily by the environmental risk and agency channels, with environmental performance being critical for investment in knowledge capital and governance performance for investment in organisational capital. The buffering effect of ESG is strongest for highly leveraged firms, where financing constraints are most binding, and for high-growth firms with abundant investment opportunities.

title: Alternative Worldviews, Distrust, and Populism
affiliations: University of Warwick and DISEIS, Faculty of Political and Social Sciences, Universita' Cattolica del Sacro Cuore

detail.title: Alternative Worldviews, Distrust, and Populism
detail.abstract: We define populism as a platform that promotes policies based on a mis-specified model of the world-a simple alternative worldview. Voters' trust in the traditional political class evolves over time, depending on the performance of mainstream politicians while in office. Crucially, political distrust increases voters' susceptibility to the alternative worldviews offered by populists. In turn, the threat of populist success disciplines traditional politicians encouraging better performance. We study when and how populists and their alternative narratives gain traction or recur, and we examine their long-run effects on voter welfare. A key feature of the model is the feedback loop between distrust and alternative truths: political distrust persists, making voters more receptive to populists even when traditional politicians improve their performance. This dynamic gives rise to a low-trust trap, where trust in mainstream politicians never fully recovers, and cycles of populist and traditional rule repeatedly emerge.

title: What DOJ's Focus On Trade Fraud Means For Companies
affiliations: University of Colorado School of Law

detail.title: What DOJ's Focus On Trade Fraud Means For Companies
detail.abstract:
The Aug. 29, 2025, launch of the interagency Trade Fraud Task Force [1] had previously signaled an invigorated focus on trade fraud enforcement as part of the administration's "America First" trade policy.
The subsequent Feb. 23 announcement, elevating trade fraud to an economic and national security imperative, will have a significant additional impact on companies in the U.S. and beyond.
For multinational corporations, importers, compliance professionals and supply chain managers, the unmistakable message is that the days of what the administration has described as laissez-faire enforcement are over.

title: Energy Dependence, Environmental Quality and Banking Sector Capital: New Evidence from OECD Countries
affiliations: Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro - Lum Enterprise s.r.l., Lum University Giuseppe Degennaro, LUM Jean Monnet university, Unicusano University and University of Catania

detail.title: Energy Dependence, Environmental Quality and Banking Sector Capital: New Evidence from OECD Countries
detail.abstract: This article seeks to explore and analyze the interrelationship between environmental factors, the structure of the energy sector, and stability/resilience within the financial sector by employing data from OECD countries between 2004 and 2021. The article utilizes new data sets provided by the World Bank Group's Global Financial Development Data and Sovereign ESG Data, with specific emphasis placed on the bank capitalization indicator, which is described as the bank capital asset ratio, and is considered an important factor in sectoral stability/resilience. Using fixed effect panel data econometrics, the article suggests that methane emissions, PM2.5 air pollution, and net energy imports have statistically significant impacts on the bank capitalization process, while renewable energy and bank capitalization have positive and statistically significant associations. The positive association between fossil fuel consumption and bank capitalization suggests that there is an inherent contradiction between current sectoral stability/resilience and the challenges associated with the energy transition process. The Hausman test suggests that omitted variables may exist and that fixed effect econometrics is an appropriate model. Clustering analysis suggests that each country has an underlying regime driven by environmental factors, the structure of the energy sector, and sectoral stability/resilience. Moreover, machine learning regression analysis employing K-Nearest Neighbors (KNN) and Random Forest models indicate that significant predictive potential is possible and that energy dependence, renewable energy, and air pollution are important factors in bank capitalization processes. The article suggests that robust evidence is provided regarding environmental quality and its interrelationship with sectoral stability/resilience and has significant implications for developing macroprudential frameworks that incorporate elements of the energy transition process.

title: Identifying Peer Firms Based on Consumer Store Visits
affiliations: Bayes Business School (formerly Cass), City, University of London and Bayes Business School, City University London

detail.title: Identifying Peer Firms Based on Consumer Store Visits
detail.abstract: We propose a novel approach to identifying economically linked peer firms based on consumers' co-visitation across retail brands. Using large-scale mobile foot-traffic and transaction data, we find that sales growth at a consumer-based peer is predictive of sales growth at the focal brand for up to six months ahead. This association strengthens with more intense shared foot traffic, closer geographic proximity, and higher local income and population density. Among public firms, these consumer-based economic links also manifest in positive associations in efficiency, profitability and valuation. In contrast, peers identified using traditional industry classifications exhibit negative associations in performance, consistent with substitution. Overall, the findings suggest that consumer co-visitation provides an additional and distinct lens for identifying economically relevant peer relationships revealed through consumers' joint demand for related products or services.

title: Robots Reinstate, AI Doesn't: Asymmetric Task Creation Across Automation Frontiers *
affiliations: Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos

detail.title: Robots Reinstate, AI Doesn't: Asymmetric Task Creation Across Automation Frontiers *
detail.abstract: Robot-exposed occupations follow V-shaped wage trajectories-decline then recoverywhile AI-exposed occupations follow L-shapes with no recovery. I develop a twofrontier task model in which the direction of automation and the rate of complementary task creation are jointly determined. Physical automation produces spatially bundled complements-maintenance, monitoring, quality control-because automated and human tasks are co-located , cognitive automation produces fewer complements because its outputs are digital and non-spatial. Calibrating the model to structurally estimated reinstatement rates identifies a complementarity ratio of 4.88: each unit of robot frontier advancement generates nearly five times as many feasible complements as AI advancement. The model also produces a directed automation trap, but the calibrated feedback is modest (7% amplification) and the economy admits a unique equilibrium. Four tests probe the predictions: (i) a 20-year ACS panel documents the V/L-shape divergence among non-college workers, predating COVID , non-college wages in robot-exposed occupations follow a V-shaped trajectory, dipping during 2010-2014 and recovering by 2018, with positive wage gains extending to all workers during the recovery phase (βR = 0.015, p = 0.006), (ii) O*NET data show robot-exposed occupations create 1.5-2 times more complementary tasks, with AI-complementary creation insignificant post-ChatGPT , (iii) robot-exposed firms expand non-AI employment while AI-adopting firms contract it , (iv) a minimum wage triple-difference finds no factor-price effect, suggesting the asymmetry is technological rather than wagedriven.

title: Ambiguity Aversion and Citizen Expectations of Government Response to UAP Reports
affiliations: Saint Mary's University, Canada

detail.title: Ambiguity Aversion and Citizen Expectations of Government Response to UAP Reports
detail.abstract: Unidentified Anomalous Phenomena (UAP) have entered formal governmental discourse in Canada, creating a policy environment characterized by institutional acknowledgment without definitive explanation. Such contexts generate ambiguity rather than measurable risk. This paper examines whether variation in ambiguity aversion predicts public expectations of government response to UAP reports. Using data from the 2025 Sky Canada Project (N = 1,008), the analysis constructs an Ambiguity Averse Epistemic Orientation (AAEO) index based on concern, security framing, and intolerance of sustained epistemic indeterminacy. Results indicate that higher ambiguity aversion is strongly associated with support for government action and public funding for investigation, even after controlling for issue salience and demographic characteristics. Disclosure expectations are also positively related to ambiguity aversion but are more sensitive to attention and engagement. A composite index of government involvement performs weakly, suggesting that public expectations are multidimensional rather than unidimensional. The findings extend ambiguity aversion theory beyond laboratory settings and demonstrate its relevance for understanding public demand for institutional escalation under acknowledged but unresolved uncertainty.

title: Egalitarian Antitrust
affiliations: Northeastern University (USA) - School of Law

detail.title: Egalitarian Antitrust

declarations.declarationOfInterest: N/A
declarations.ethicsApproval: N/A
declarations.funderStatement: N/A

detail.abstract:
Egalitarian political thought can re-center antitrust law toward its social mission at a time of growing inequality and economic consolidation. Seen through an egalitarian lens, antitrust has social function: to rectify monopolistic excesses, to remove barriers to opportunity, and to structure markets in line with justice and equality. 

Drawing on foundational work in political theory, this Article clarifies what antitrust law can contribute to justice, democracy and equality going forward. It addresses current disagreements in the field of antitrust law, such as whether monopoly and affordability concerns should have a prominent place in antitrust or can be trumped by efficiency and pro-business considerations, and what antitrust's relation to other regulatory and legal domains should be. The Article situates these and other issues within longstanding debates in political theory and highlights the role of democratic institutions and competitive markets as constraints on concentrated political and economic power. 

Egalitarian thought suggests three directions for antitrust reform: (a) enhancing the clarity, accessibility and democratic character of antitrust law institutions, opinions and procedures; (b) promoting equitable and egalitarian antitrust interventions in markets that prioritize workers and small businesses; and (c) situating antitrust law within a broader constellation of regulatory tools.

title: The Macroeconomics of Asymmetric Automation: Frontier Technologies, Productivity, and the Labor Share
affiliations: Universidad Nacional Mayor de San Marcos

detail.title: The Macroeconomics of Asymmetric Automation: Frontier Technologies, Productivity, and the Labor Share
detail.abstract: Automation technologies differ in their capacity to generate complementary human tasks. I build a two-frontier growth model in which physical and cognitive automation advance simultaneously but reinstate labor at different rates. The cognitive reinstatement rate is structurally estimated from U.S. commuting-zone wage data. Robot automation generates approximately 31 percent more aggregate productivity per unit of frontier advance than AI, driven almost entirely by differential task creation and reallocation rather than direct displacement. Three macro results follow. First, both frontiers lower the labor share, but robots are 42 percent as damaging as AI per unit of advance. Second, distributional consequences are supply-side dominant; aggregate demand channels are second-order. Third, the optimal R&D subsidy favors robots over AI at approximately 1.6-to-one, reflecting both efficiency and equity motives. A uniform automation tax is welfare-reducing. * I am grateful to James Heckman for guidance and support. All errors are my own.

title: From Gaps to Gains: Empowering Indian Youth Workforce with Skill Development
affiliations: University of Southampton

detail.title: From Gaps to Gains: Empowering Indian Youth Workforce with Skill Development

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethics approval for the secondary data used was obtained from the University of Southampton ethics committee.
declarations.funderStatement: ESRC South Coast Doctoral Training Partnership funded the research, which is part of my PhD project at the University of Southampton.

keywords: Vocational and Technical Training JEL Classification: J24

detail.abstract: For decades, the unemployment problem has significantly affected the youth labour force in India, and it is reflected in their underperformance in the labour market. Vocational and technical training (VTT) is considered one of the measures to tackle this issue by improving their skill level. This research aims to analyse the impact of VTT (which prepares an individual to become more employable) on labour market outcomes using the Periodic Labour Force Survey in India. Since the assignment of training is nonrandom, I use an instrumental variable to capture the specific social network of the individuals that is highly correlated with the probability of training but does not directly affect the probability of employment. The Instrumental Variable (IV) results indicate that participation in training is associated with a 19.2 percentage point increase in the probability of employment for the 15-to 35-year-old age group. Moreover, the Conditional Recursive Mixed-Process (CMP) method, which addresses the endogeneity and sample selection issues in the returns-to-training model, shows around 40.4% higher wages for the trained individuals.

title: Private Health Insurance and Financial Protection Against Catastrophic Maternal and Child Healthcare Expenditure in Zambia
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Private Health Insurance and Financial Protection Against Catastrophic Maternal and Child Healthcare Expenditure in Zambia
detail.abstract: Background: The cost of maternal and child health care can create a barrier that may lead to financial distress and poor health outcomes. This paper investigates the extent to which private health insurance provides financial protection against catastrophic maternal and child health care expenditures in Zambia.  Methods: Analyses were conducted using data gathered as part of a 2014 Zambia Household Health Expenditure and Utilization Survey. This paper adopts the Ataguba method for analysing catastrophic expenditures against the capacity to pay. The main research question was investigated using the eteffects endogenous treatment effects model. Results: This paper provides evidence of potential financial distress due to maternal and child expenditure in Zambia. The results show that antenatal care results in the highest incidences of catastrophic expenditures compared to delivery and postnatal care. On the other hand, the intensity of the catastrophe is highest for delivery care expenditure than it is for antenatal or postnatal care expenditure. In addition, the findings in this paper indicate that health insurance is more likely to provide financial protection from catastrophic aggregate, antenatal, delivery and postnatal care expenditures.   Conclusion: The paper provides empirical evidence of catastrophic maternal and child care expenditures in Zambia. In addition, the paper highlights that health insurance reduces the likelihood of women incurring catastrophic antenatal, delivery and postnatal care expenses. Therefore, an increase in private health insurance coverage can lead to better financial protection outcomes, especially for mothers seeking maternal and child health care services.

title: Local Taxes and Suburbanization: Evidence from Philadelphia's Wage Tax
affiliations: and Harvard University

detail.title: Local Taxes and Suburbanization: Evidence from Philadelphia's Wage Tax
detail.abstract: How do local taxes affect the location of economic activity inside cities? We study Philadelphia's wage tax, which applies to residents regardless of where they work and to suburban residents who work in the city. Because city residents always pay the tax, it does not distort their workplace choices, whereas suburban residents are penalized only for working in Philadelphia. At the city boundary, rising wage tax rates should sharply reduce commuting to the city in suburban tracts relative to neighboring city tracts, while falling tax rates should increase it. Using a spatial regression discontinuity design, we find that as the wage tax rose from 1.5 to 4.3% between 1960 and 1980, the change in the proportion of residents working in the city fell sharply in suburban tracts just outside the boundary; as the tax fell to 3.4% between 2003 and 2019, the change in that proportion increased sharply in the same tracts. Similar results hold along the boundaries of other cities with wage tax variation, such as Detroit and Cleveland, but not in cities without wage taxes. In our preferred estimate, a 1% increase in the tax rate reduces suburb-to-city commuting by 6.39%, holding wages, rents, and amenities constant. We embed this elasticity in a quantitative spatial model to estimate how the wage tax affects suburbanization once wages and rents adjust. Replacing the wage tax with a non-distortionary land value tax would bring 26,000 jobs from the suburbs into Philadelphia. Such gains triple when we allow for productivity agglomeration forces.

detail.abstract: I study the credit channel of the electric-vehicle (EV) transition using more than 1.8 million German auto loans and leases. I show that EV financing contracts default significantly less often than comparable internal combustion engine vehicle (ICEV) contracts-particularly among lower-income borrowers. Following the 2020 expansion of German federal EV subsidies, lenders adjusted EV financing relative to comparable ICEV contracts. Independent banks tightened EV loan terms while lending to lower-income borrowers. Captive banks also tightened EV loans, mainly through non-price terms, while accommodating subsidy-period EV demand more readily through leasing.

title: The Impact of COVID-19 on SDG 2 -Zero Hunger: Challenges to Balance IP Protection with Food Security

detail.abstract: The COVID-19 pandemic posed a multifaceted and unprecedented worldwide challenge with profound implications for food security. This study examines the multifaceted impact of COVID-19 on food security, addressing the challenges it has presented, the responses undertaken at national and international levels, and valuable lessons learned during these challenging times. The pandemic disrupted every aspect of food security, affecting food access, availability, stability, and utilization. The research study's objective is to examine COVID-19's effects on food security. The investigation was conducted on a worldwide scale, with a particular emphasis on nations experiencing food insecurity. Toward this end, the data is used from different sources such as the Food Agricultural Organization (FAO), recent report on the State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World 2023, and the Global Report on Food Crises (GRFC) 2023. The study's finding shows that COVID-19 has had a massive impact on food supply chains, hunger, international food trade, food prices, nutritional food, and agricultural labour shortage. Due to their heavy reliance on securing their food supplies, developing countries are disproportionately affected by the food security challenges resulting from COVID-19. In addition, the pandemic has emphasized the critical role of international collaboration and the imperative of addressing underlying vulnerabilities in global food supply chains during the crises. This paper also evaluates the impact of intellectual property protection for plant varieties on food security and SDG 2. Based on the findings, a few recommendations have been made that could help increase sustainable food security.

title: Corporate Integrity and Corporate Cash Reserves: Insights from Textual Analysis
affiliations: The University of Western Australia, Pennsylvania State University - School of Graduate Professional Studies (SGPS) and Monash University - Department of Banking and Finance

detail.title: Corporate Integrity and Corporate Cash Reserves: Insights from Textual Analysis
detail.abstract: We examine how corporate integrity influences firms' liquidity policies. Using a large U.S. sample and a text-based measure of corporate integrity developed by Li et al. (2021) from earnings call transcripts, we analyze whether an ethical corporate culture affects cash-holding behavior. The results show that firms with higher integrity maintain significantly larger cash reserves, consistent with the safety-net hypothesis that integrity-oriented managers adopt more cautious and riskaverse financial policies. The findings remain robust across alternative specifications, including propensity score matching, entropy balancing, and instrumental-variable analyses. Moreover, the effect is stronger among highly leveraged firms, suggesting that integrity reinforces financial prudence when external risk is greater. Overall, the evidence highlights corporate integrity as an important and stable driver of liquidity management, stressing its role in promoting financial resilience and sound risk management.

title: Nourishing Minds: The Impact of Healthy School Lunches on Student Wellbeing
affiliations: Victoria University of Wellington - Te Herenga Waka - School of Economics & Finance and Deakin University - School of Education

detail.title: Nourishing Minds: The Impact of Healthy School Lunches on Student Wellbeing
detail.abstract: We evaluate the impacts of the New Zealand Healthy School Lunches Program (HSLP), a government program that provides nutritionally balanced meals to all students in schools identified as containing the 25 percent most disadvantaged students. students. Exploiting the program's eligibility threshold, we estimate the causal effects of the HSLP on self-reported wellbeing using a regression discontinuity design. We find the program increases pediatric quality-of-life scores by around 8% and, more importantly, reduces the probability that a student is classified as "at risk" for impaired pediatric quality of life by 40%. We also find comparable improvements in Māori wellbeing (Hua Oranga) and WHO-5 wellbeing scores. Across measures, these effects correspond to approximately 0.3 standard deviations. The impacts are substantially larger-around 0.4 standard deviations-among students who lack regular access to adequate food at home, suggesting particularly high the benefits of healthy school lunches for food-insecure students.

title: Dynamic Arbitrage from Price-Based Risk Constraints
affiliations: BI Norwegian Business School and Warwick Business School

detail.title: Dynamic Arbitrage from Price-Based Risk Constraints
detail.abstract: Under classic no-manipulation conditions on market impact, price-based risk constraints (margins, haircuts, leverage limits, volatility targets, mandates) can still generate dynamic arbitrage. We develop a refined no-dynamic-arbitrage test for such environments; it requires only the constraint rule and an estimate of market impact. The test also yields an upper bound on the size of the constrained sector consistent with non-manipulability. We apply it to volatility-managed portfolios: admissible scale is well below one day of average daily volume and below 1% of the size of the underlying market, while vulnerability rises sharply once linked notional reaches roughly one to two days of daily volume, or about 1% to 2% of underlying market size. Manipulation incentives are strongest in low-volatility states, driven by feedback between measured risk and rule-induced trading.

title: Artificial Superintelligence May be Useless: Equilibria in the Economy of Multiple AI Agents
affiliations: Cornell College, University of Iowa, Iowa City Math Circle and Club,  and Shandong University - Center for Economic Research

detail.title: Artificial Superintelligence May be Useless: Equilibria in the Economy of Multiple AI Agents
detail.abstract: With recent development of artificial intelligence, it is more common to adopt AI agents in economic activities. This paper explores the economic actions of agents, including human agents and AI agents, in an economic game of trading products/services, and the equilibria in this economy involving multiple agents. We derive a range of equilibrium results and their corresponding conditions using a Markov chain stationary distribution based model. One distinct feature of our model is that we consider the long-term utility generated by economic activities instead of their short-term benefits. For the model consisting of two agents, we fully characterize all the possible economic equilibria and conditions. Interestingly, we show that unless each agent can at least double (not merely increase) its marginal utility by purchasing the other agent's products/services, purchasing the other agent's products/services will not happen in any economic equilibrium. We further extend our results to three and more agents, where we characterize more economic equilibria. We find that in some equilibria, the "more powerful" AI agents contribute zero utility to "less capable" agents.

title: Who Pays for Clean Power? Evidence on Public Support and Solar Adoption Frictions in Mexico
affiliations: Stanford University, University of Florida, Centro de Investigación y Docencia Económicas (CIDE) - Division of Economics and

detail.title: Who Pays for Clean Power? Evidence on Public Support and Solar Adoption Frictions in Mexico
detail.abstract: This article investigates the political economy of energy transition in Mexico, a country with vast solar potential but distorted electricity markets. Using randomized survey experiments, we analyze the drivers of public support for utility-scale renewables and the adoption of private residential solar (PV). The results reveal a "green support gap": clean energy backing is high but highly elastic to tariff surcharges. Regarding private adoption, we find sub-additivity between upfront subsidies and long-term savings, an effect attenuated for low-income households, suggesting liquidity constraints dictate distinct incentive-stacking logics. Furthermore, using propensity score matching, we document massive informational friction: realized bill savings among adopters are 152% higher than non-adopters' expectations. This pessimism bias-underestimating benefits by a factor of 2.5-creates an intention-action gap that limits price-based interventions. We conclude that accelerating solar adoption requires a coordinated policy mix addressing retail price distortions, liquidity constraints, and informational frictions in emerging economies facing fiscal and climate trade-offs.

title: When Do Habits Matter? The Empirical Content of Dynamic Hedonic Models

detail.title: When Do Habits Matter? The Empirical Content of Dynamic Hedonic Models
detail.abstract: Hedonic models value goods through their characteristics but are typically interpreted under time-separable preferences. This assumption is restrictive: when some attributes are habit forming, observed prices reflect both contemporaneous utility and continuation values from past consumption. I develop a nonparametric revealed preference framework for dynamic hedonic valuation, deriving necessary and sufficient conditions for rationalisability over characteristics. The framework separates restrictions imposed by the hedonic price system from those imposed by intertemporal choice and provides diagnostics that quantify the severity of violations along each margin. Applied to household scanner data, I show that most failures of static hedonic valuation reflect violations of the hedonic price structure; conditional on satisfying this structure, allowing for habit formation improves behavioural fit. This alters the mapping from prices to willingness-to-pay and the implied welfare interpretation.

title: Great (Retirement) Expectations: A Review of Retirement Income Policy and Changes to Expected and Preferred Retirement Age of Australian Workers
affiliations: The University of Western Australia - UWA Business School, The University of Western Australia and Macquarie University

detail.title: Great (Retirement) Expectations: A Review of Retirement Income Policy and Changes to Expected and Preferred Retirement Age of Australian Workers

declarations.funderStatement: This research was co‐funded by the Australian Research Council, Linkage Project (LP190100574) and Allianz Retire+. Open access publishing facilitated by The University of Western Australia, as part of the Wiley ‐ The University of Western Australia agreement via the Council of Australian University Librarians.

detail.abstract: Research Question/Issue: Retirement age expectations and preferences are shaped by individual, social, and government policy influences. Our paper reviews major policy changes in the Australian Retirement Income System over the past two decades and documents changes in Australian workers' expected and preferred retirement age. Research Findings/Insights: We identify three key results. First, workers prefer to retire earlier than they expect to, on average. Second, both expected and preferred retirement age increased through the 2000s and 2010s but stalled from 2017. Third, a significant proportion of workers do not know when they expect to retire. Practitioner/Policy Implications: In the absence of the ability to set a mandatory retirement age, a key objective of retirement policy has been to raise retirement age. Our results suggest that while workers' expectations and preferences reflect this, they have stalled somewhat. Further, a small but persistent proportion of workers do not form expectations which, given its importance in successful workforce exit plans and retirement wellbeing, presents a key challenge. Methods Used: We describe changes in policy over the past two decades before describing patterns and dynamics in retirement age expectations and preferences of workers aged 45-60, 2003-2023 using the Household, Income and Labour Dynamics in Australia (HILDA) Survey.

title: Integrating Subsurface Geothermal Assessment with Surface Energy Planning: A Multidisciplinary Methodology for Heat Network Development
affiliations: , University of Leeds, University of Leeds, University of Oxford - Lincoln College, University of Leeds, University of Leeds, University of Leeds - Sustainability Research Institute, University of Leeds, University of Leeds and University of Leeds

detail.title: Integrating Subsurface Geothermal Assessment with Surface Energy Planning: A Multidisciplinary Methodology for Heat Network Development

declarations.ethicsApproval: Ethical approval for the interviews and workshop was granted by the University of Leeds Research Ethics Committee.
declarations.funderStatement: This work was supported by the University of Leeds and Research England Policy Support funding.

detail.abstract: Heat zoning frameworks emerging across Europe assess heat demand and network viability using surface-level indicators but lack subsurface geothermal resource data. Separately, geological assessments of urban geothermal potential are rarely connected to energy planning or stakeholder decision-making. This paper presents a multidisciplinary methodology which bridges these domains, combining geological modelling, geospatial energy analysis, GIS-based spatial integration, and stakeholder co-design through a decision theatre. The methodology translates probabilistic geological estimates into planning-compatible formats, overlays them with building stock, heat demand and development data to identify spatial alignments and mismatches, and tests integrated proposals through structured stakeholder engagement. We applied this across three contrasting zones in Leeds, UK: an established city centre with existing district heating, a greenfield development area, and a mixed existing settlement. In each case, the integrated methodology generated context-sensitive proposals which no single-domain analysis could provide. In the city centre, it revealed a viable geothermal resource beneath an incumbent network whose commercial model could not accommodate it. This led to proposals for new networks beyond the existing system. In the greenfield zone, overlaying subsurface potential with the development pipeline revealed a closing temporal window, with homes being consented above viable aquifers using incompatible heating systems. In the existing settlement, the methodology identified misclassified anchor loads that altered the viability assessment for network development. These findings demonstrate that integrating subsurface and surface data within planning processes reveals resource opportunities, development conflicts and implementation barriers invisible when geological assessment and energy planning are conducted independently. The integration logic is transferable to contexts where geological and surface-level planning data are available.

title: How Much Can I Make? Cross-Firm Pay Transparency's Effects On the US Labor Market
affiliations: and The University of Texas at Austin, TX, USA

detail.title: How Much Can I Make? Cross-Firm Pay Transparency's Effects On the US Labor Market
detail.abstract: Many major US jurisdictions have implemented pay transparency laws that require firms to advertise wage offers in vacancy postings. Using data on the near universe of job postings and representative survey data in a difference-indifferences framework, we find that these laws increased the fraction of postings with wage information by 24.7 percentage points. This translated to average real wage increases of 3.2%-4.4% in Colorado and 0.6%-1.3% in California and Washington. We further consistently find significant positive effects on real wages for workers who are male, have a college-degree, or are over forty years old.

title: Forward Guidance for Skeptical Markets

detail.title: Forward Guidance for Skeptical Markets
detail.abstract: This paper develops a theory of forward guidance that captures two key features of central bank communication: announcements are not fully state-contingent, and the private sector is wary of policy mistakes. The central bank tailors announcements along two dimensions: (i) vagueness-how tightly the announcement constrains future policy; and (ii) data dependence-how aggressively future policy responds to a public signal of the economy. Three main lessons emerge. First, uncertainty affects communication differently depending on its source: uncertainty about both demand and cost-push shocks increases optimal vagueness, but only demand-side uncertainty increases the optimal degree of data dependence. Second, strict rules are costly: fully precise guidance entails sizable welfare losses that grow with the steepness of the Phillips curve. Third, because of the stabilizing role of announcements, optimal forward guidance differs sharply from simply communicating the best forecast of the future optimal policy rate (Delphic guidance).

title: Artificial Intelligence and Rent Sharing Between Airlines and Workers: Evidence from the U.S. Airline Industry
affiliations: Purdue University and University of British Columbia (UBC) - Sauder School of Business

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence and Rent Sharing Between Airlines and Workers: Evidence from the U.S. Airline Industry
detail.abstract: Has the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution already begun to reshape the airline labor market? Following the COVID-19 pandemic, airline workers experienced rapid wage increases amid acute labor shortages. At the same time, the emergence of generative AI after 2022 introduced new technological expectations that may have altered bargaining conditions. This study examines how the distribution of quasi-rents between airlines and workers has evolved over the period 2000-2024. We construct feasible wage benchmarks based on a Nash rent-sharing framework and embed them within a two-tier stochastic frontier model to measure deviations from these benchmarks. This approach allows us to quantify how observed wages reflect shifts in surplus distribution rather than changes in wage levels alone. The results reveal a long-run decline in worker-side rent extraction, with a pronounced shift after 2022. Despite rising wages and continued labor market tightness following the COVID-19 recovery, observed wages increasingly fall below feasible benchmarks, indicating that airlines retain a growing share of quasi-rents. An occupation-weighted AI exposure index, interpreted as a measure of expected technological substitution, shows that higher exposure is associated with larger worker-side wage shortfalls relative to the benchmark. This pattern is particularly pronounced at low-cost carriers, where more standardized operations generate broader exposure across routine cognitive tasks. Overall, the findings suggest that technological expectations associated with generative AI may 2 have already shifted bargaining outcomes in favor of airlines, even in the presence of labor shortages. The study contributes to the literature by providing the first empirical evidence linking AI-related exposure to rent-sharing dynamics in the airline industry within a unified bargainingfrontier framework, highlighting the distributional implications of technological change.

title: Targeting, Personalization, and Engagement in an Agricultural Advisory Service
affiliations: Stanford Graduate School of Business, Harvard Business School, University of Georgia and

detail.title: Targeting, Personalization, and Engagement in an Agricultural Advisory Service
detail.abstract:
We conduct a series of iterative experiments to evaluate approaches for optimally targeting calls for an agricultural advisory service serving over one million farmers in rural India. We estimate the value of alternative targeted policies using “off-policy” evaluation on data from randomized call assignments. When we evaluate off-policy using held-out data from the same time periods used to design the targeted policies, we find that targeted policies increase engagement by up to 8%. However, when we design a policy using current data and then implement the policy for randomly selected users in subsequent weeks, our “on-policy” evaluation estimates show realized gains that are substantially smaller. We develop tools to diagnose the causes of this underperformance and adopt a transfer-learning approach to policy learning and off-policy evaluation that accounts for temporal changes in farmer behavior, substantially improving off-policy estimates of performance in subsequent weeks. We further develop novel approaches to targeted policy design that respond to organizational objectives and resource constraints, including distributional goals (e.g., reaching women farmers) and prioritizing farmers likely to benefit most from the information on downstream outcomes (e.g., yields). We propose a method for organizations to quantify trade-offs between objectives, and we demonstrate the value of targeting for alleviating these trade-offs.

title: Easy A’s, Less Pay: The Long-Term Effects of Grade Inflation
affiliations: University of Texas at Austin, RAND Corporation,  and University of Georgia

detail.title: Easy A’s, Less Pay: The Long-Term Effects of Grade Inflation
detail.abstract:
Average grades continue to rise in the United States, raising the question of how grade inflation impacts students. We provide comprehensive evidence on how teacher grading practices affect students' long-run success. Using administrative high school data from Los Angeles and from Maryland that is linked to postsecondary and earnings records, we develop and validate two teacher-level measures of grade inflation: one measuring average grade inflation and another measuring a teacher's propensity to give a passing grade. These measures of grade inflation are distinct from teacher value-added, with grade inflating teachers having moderately lower cognitive value-added and slightly higher noncognitive value-added. These two measures also differentially impact students' long-term outcomes. Being assigned a higher average grade inflating teacher reduces a student's future test scores, the likelihood of graduating from high school, college enrollment, and ultimately earnings. In contrast, passing grade inflation reduces the likelihood of being held back and increases high school graduation, with limited long-run effects. The cumulative impact is economically significant: a teacher with one standard deviation higher average grade inflation reduces the present discounted value of lifetime earnings of their students by $213,872 per year.

title: Creative Pathways: The Potential of Music to Support Strengths-based Approaches to Youth Justice in Australia
affiliations: Griffith University - Queensland Conservatorium, Griffith University, Griffith University and Griffith University

detail.title: Creative Pathways: The Potential of Music to Support Strengths-based Approaches to Youth Justice in Australia
detail.abstract: Youth justice systems in Australia are in urgent need of innovative programs to address entrenched inequity, high rates of recidivism, and wellbeing concerns. In seeking effective alternatives to detention, scholars and community members have called for strengths-based investments in primary prevention programs to complement or counter more established risk-based youth justice paradigms. Considering how youth themselves may be positioned as resources to meet their own needs, this article presents a scoping review of 19 international studies to consider how music programs might support such strengths-based strategies in Australia and internationally. The outcomes reported in these studies focus on individual and interpersonal domains and suggest that music-based programs promote self-awareness and identity construction, wellbeing, engagement in learning and skill-acquisition, interpersonal awareness, a sense of belonging, and can enhance communication and relationship building skills. The findings of this scoping review demonstrate the potential of music programs to enhance preventative practices and desistance strategies and provide powerful resources for strengths-based approaches to youth justice.

title: Tuition, Transfer, and Turmoil: Understanding the Dynamics of For-Profit College Shutdowns

detail.title: Tuition, Transfer, and Turmoil: Understanding the Dynamics of For-Profit College Shutdowns
detail.abstract: Between 2015 and 2018, several of the nation's largest for-profit college chains abruptly collapsed, disrupting the education of over 200,000 students. In the year before failure, these schools raised tuition by nearly $1,000, eight times their typical annual increase, while most continuing students stayed put until the day of closure. This striking inelasticity reveals high switching costs that leave students "locked in," unable to escape even as prices spike. After closure, students overwhelmingly reallocate to nearby community colleges, highlighting the public sector's role as a safety net. To interpret these dynamics and design effective policy, I estimate a dynamic college-choice model in which forward-looking students face heterogeneous switching costs and form expectations about potential closures. The model explains both the muted response to pre-closure tuition hikes and the chaotic, forced transfers that follow. Counterfactuals show that tuition freezes alone provide limited protection and can even backfire, keeping prices low and drawing new students into failing schools. By contrast, policies that lower switching costs, such as universal credit transfer or targeted transfer grants, and increase transparency about institutional distress generate large welfare gains. These interventions encourage proactive, voluntary transfers, curbing the disruptive wave of last-minute moves when schools collapse. My results show that protecting students requires mobility and information, not just price regulation. Reducing switching costs tackles the root problem, preventing predatory pricing and minimizing the fallout when higher education institutions fail.

title: Autonomous AI Agents for Option Hedging: Enhancing Financial Stability through Shortfall Aware Reinforcement Learning
affiliations: Cornell University, University of Texas, Nanyang Technological University and Johns Hopkins University

detail.title: Autonomous AI Agents for Option Hedging: Enhancing Financial Stability through Shortfall Aware Reinforcement Learning

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare that they have no known competing financial interests or personal relationships that could have appeared to influence the work reported in this paper.

detail.abstract: The deployment of autonomous AI agents in derivatives markets has widened a practical gap between static model calibration and realized hedging outcomes. We introduce two reinforcement learning frameworks, a novel Replication Learning of Option Pricing (RLOP) approach and an adaptive extension of Q-learner in Black-Scholes (QLBS), that prioritize shortfall probability and align learning objectives with downside sensitive hedging. Using listed SPY and XOP options, we evaluate models using realized path delta hedging outcome distributions, shortfall probability, and tail risk measures such as Expected Shortfall. Empirically, RLOP reduces shortfall frequency in most slices and shows the clearest tail-risk improvements in stress, while implied volatility fit often favors parametric models yet poorly predicts after-cost hedging performance. This friction-aware RL framework supports a practical approach to autonomous derivatives risk management as AI-augmented trading systems scale.

title: When War Becomes a Financial Instrument

detail.title: When War Becomes a Financial Instrument
detail.abstract: The escalation of military conflict involving the United States, Israel, and Iran in early 2026 has triggered an unprecedented cluster of force majeure declarations across energy contracts, shipping obligations, and infrastructure investment commitments in the Gulf region. While force majeure provisions allow commercial delivery obligations to be suspended under conditions of war or political disruption, the underlying financing obligations embedded in project finance structures remain legally absolute. This article introduces Debt Service Asymmetry as a structural feature of project finance systems in which commercial contract relief under force majeure does not extend to financing obligations, creating systemic stress during geopolitical disruptions. Drawing on EMEA project finance data, FIDIC contract law, institutional reports, and comparative case studies of the Ever Given/Suez Canal disruption (2021) and the Red Sea Houthi attacks (2023-2025), the article examines how force majeure operates within the legal architecture of international infrastructure finance. It argues that the force majeure declarations emerging from the 2026 Hormuz crisis represent a qualitative shift: a legal instrument originally designed to manage commercial risk is increasingly being deployed as a tool of sovereign geopolitical signalling. The analysis suggests that this dynamic exposes a structural vulnerability within global project finance systems, particularly in energy-exporting regions where sovereign revenue stability underpins large-scale infrastructure investment. The implications extend beyond the Gulf to the broader Middle East-Africa infrastructure corridor, where future investment frameworks may need to address the unresolved tension between commercial force majeure relief and the continuity of debt service obligations.

title: The Economics of Algorithmic Personalization: Evidence from an Educational Technology Platform
affiliations: Stanford University, Stanford Graduate School of Business, Stanford University, University of Georgia and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: The Economics of Algorithmic Personalization: Evidence from an Educational Technology Platform
detail.abstract:
Can personalized recommendations improve engagement in educational technology? We design, test, and scale a collaborative filtering system for Freadom, an English-learning app for Indian children. A randomized controlled trial (RCT) with 7,750 students shows that personalization, deployed in a single content section, increases engagement by 60% in that section and by 14% app-wide. We then exploit an eligibility threshold in a regression discontinuity design (RDD) to track effects over five months of deployment. For user cohorts receiving personalization during deployment, RDD estimates exceed RCT benchmark by a factor of 2.5, opposite of the “voltage drop" typically observed in policy scale-ups. This provides evidence that, for algorithmic interventions, RCT estimates may be lower bounds on scaled impact rather than upper bounds. However, personalization benefits are front-loaded. Gains concentrate in users’ first weeks, with diminishing returns thereafter. This pattern, combined with the sharp decline in predicted match quality as users exhaust their best content matches, suggests that content availability rather than algorithmic sophistication becomes the binding constraint.

title: Why Financial Openness Alone Cannot Stabilise African Economies

detail.title: Why Financial Openness Alone Cannot Stabilise African Economies
detail.abstract: This article argues that financial openness, by itself, is neither a sufficient nor a reliable stabilisation mechanism for African economies. While capital account liberalisation is often promoted as a pathway to macroeconomic resilience, its stabilising effects are highly conditional on complementary domestic capabilities, most notably institutional quality, financial depth, countercyclical fiscal capacity, credible exchange-rate regimes, and effective macroprudential policy. In the absence of these complements, financial openness can amplify exposure to commodity price fluctuations and global financial cycles, intensify exchange-rate volatility, and transmit capital-flow volatility into growth instability. Drawing on a synthesis of crosscountry and Africa-specific empirical evidence, the article reframes financial openness as a sequencing and capacity problem rather than a binary policy choice. The evidence suggests that openness functions as a lever whose stabilising payoff depends on domestic shock-absorption capacity, not as a panacea capable of insulating African economies from external volatility.

title: AI in Science
affiliations: University of Toronto - Rotman School of Management, University of Galway and Georgia Institute of Technology - Strategic Management Area

detail.title: AI in Science
detail.abstract:
We explore the impact of artificial intelligence (AI) on the knowledge production function. We characterize AI as a tool, not for full automation but rather for augmentation through enhanced search over combinatorial spaces. This leads to increased scientific productivity. We decompose knowledge production into a multi-stage process to shed light on the "jagged frontier" of AI in science, revealing differential returns to different tools across domains (e.g., data-rich biology vs. anomaly-sparse physics) and workflow stages (e.g., strong design aids like AlphaFold vs. subtler question generation tools). We treat human judgment as indispensable for tasks involving abductive inference, contextual nuance, and trade-offs, particularly in data-sparse environments. Drawing on a task-based model that distinguishes "ordinary" from AI-expert scientists, we describe how exogenous improvements in AI yield nonlinear productivity gains amplified by the share of scientists that are AI-experts to underscore the role of AI complements like skills training and organizational design.
