title: The Canadian Pension System - Assessing Coverage, Efficiency, and Long-Term Sustainability
affiliations: Dalarna University

detail.title: The Canadian Pension System - Assessing Coverage, Efficiency, and Long-Term Sustainability

declarations.declarationOfInterest: I am currently a Master's student at Dalarna University, Sweden, and this research paper was submitted for my Applied Microeconomics assignment.

detail.abstract:
Canada’s pension system stands out as one of balance and pragmatism. It’s a structure built on three solid pillars, Old Age Security (OAS)/Guaranteed Income Supplement (GIS), Canada Pension Plan (CPP)/ Quebec Pension Plan (QPP), and private or voluntary savings, that together provide most Canadians with a measure of financial security in old age. The system’s mixed design reflects a deliberate compromise between universality and contribution-based fairness, and it’s served the country well. However, the system is starting to show signs of weakness. Coverage gaps persist for women, immigrants, and non-standard workers, and the slow but steady march of population aging continues to tighten the fiscal resources. This research paper reveals that even well-designed systems cannot remain stagnant in the face of shifting demographics and work patterns. 

With the share of seniors nearing one in five Canadians, the system’s long-term health depends on adaptability, on small, steady adjustments rather than grand overhauls. Keeping that balance between compassion and discipline, between today’s retirees and tomorrow’s taxpayers, will determine whether Canada can continue to call its pension model both fair and sustainable in the decades to come.

title: Carbon Disclosure Practices And Financial Performance: Evidence From Selected Companies Listed On The National Stock Exchange Of India

detail.title: Carbon Disclosure Practices And Financial Performance: Evidence From Selected Companies Listed On The National Stock Exchange Of India
detail.abstract: Climate change has emerged as one of the most pressing global challenges of the 21 st century, as governments, regulators, and stakeholders increasingly emphasis environmental sustainability. Corporations are expected to adopt responsible environmental practices and disclose information on carbon emissions and climate-related strategies. In this context, carbon disclosure has gained significant attention as an important mechanism through which firms communicate their environmental performance and sustainability initiatives to stakeholders.

title: Train in Vain: A Review of Monopoly Politics by Erik Peinert
affiliations: George Mason University - Antonin Scalia Law School

detail.title: Train in Vain: A Review of Monopoly Politics by Erik Peinert
detail.abstract: In his new book, Monopoly Politics: Competition and Learning in the Evolution of Policy Regimes, Erik Peinert seeks to explain long-run changes in competition policy in the United States and France. He develops a fairly complicated theory that draws on insights from several academic fields, but its key elements are drawn from psychology, with policymakers' cognitive failures generating swings in policy between support for competition and monopoly. Although Peinert's work is ambitious, Monopoly Politics is more likely to be influential for its methodology than for its success in explaining the evolution of competition policy.

title: The Federated Sovereign Wealth Fund: A Case Study of America's Foreign Policy-Making Through the Capital Markets
affiliations: Penn State University

detail.title: The Federated Sovereign Wealth Fund: A Case Study of America's Foreign Policy-Making Through the Capital Markets

publicationDetails.detailsText: Creighton International and Comparative Law Journal (Forthcoming in 2026)

detail.abstract: Is “buying” Greenland the only way the United States can address its need for rare earths? Or can the United States utilize the global capital markets to advance national interests, including securing reliable critical minerals supply chains and supporting broader foreign policy objectives? This article addresses these questions by examining what the author terms the “federated” sovereign wealth fund (“federated SWF”)—a system that, while not formally declared by the U.S. government, has effectively materialized through existing federal investment practices. In contrast to traditional centralized sovereign wealth funds, this emerging structure reflects a distributed investment architecture operating across multiple federal actors and policy channels. To the extent the model relies on market participation rather than territorial acquisition or direct resource control, it also illustrates how state investment can function as a stabilizing and non-coercive instrument of national strategy, even if geopolitical competition remains present.

title: Stagflation Risk and Financial Markets: A Real-Time Composite Index
affiliations: University of Colorado at Denver - Department of Finance

detail.title: Stagflation Risk and Financial Markets: A Real-Time Composite Index
detail.abstract: This paper constructs a novel Composite Stagflation Index designed to serve as a practical tool for policymakers and researchers monitoring stagflationary risk in real time. The index combines two components: a fundamental proxy aggregating inflation, unemployment, and GDP growth, and a sentiment component derived from Google Trends capturing geopolitical supply disruptions. The index exhibits high persistence across all components. The central finding is a strong inverse relationship between the stagflation index and stock market returns, with an economic significance of-57.0%, and a direct relationship with market volatility, with economic significance of 6.6%. Stagflation thus substantially depresses returns while amplifying market uncertainty. The index further significantly increases both the Economic Policy Uncertainty index and the Partisan Conflict Index. Forward-looking analyses reveal a small and insignificant impact on future returns but a large, persistent, and highly significant effect on future market volatility across 1-, 3-, and 6-month horizons. Stagflation risk is primarily priced through the volatility channel rather than predictable return dynamics.

title: Revisiting Thailand's Phillips Curves: A Granular Panel Data Approach
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Revisiting Thailand's Phillips Curves: A Granular Panel Data Approach
detail.abstract: This paper employs disaggregated panel data to examine the evolution of Thailand’s Phillips Curve (PC) before and during the pandemic, providing empirical evidence on the nature of Thai inflation dynamics and their implications for optimal monetary policy formulation. Utilizing the real output gap derived from various methodologies, the findings reveal a relatively flat PC for Thailand, with a slightly steeper curve after COVID-19. In addition to domestic demand, external demand—reflected through global energy prices and food prices—played a significant role in Thailand’s inflation dynamics. The Thai PC exhibits both backward-looking and forward-looking behavior, with a more weight on inertia parts. In addition to the price PC, the empirical evidence supports the presence of a wage PC, with coefficients comparable in magnitude to those for non-tradable inflation, suggesting that wage dynamics constitute a driver of non-tradable price developments. Meanwhile, staggered real wage setting is found to contribute to the backward-looking component of Thai inflation. Under an optimal inflation-targeting monetary policy, greater weight is placed on closing the inflation gap during normal periods, with even more emphasis during high-inflation episodes. This result, however, does not hold when the output gap is measured using the HP filter in the policy optimization.

title: Financial System Resilience and Credit Heterogeneity:,A Comparative Analysis of Consumer Credit and Microfinance in Peru (2004–2025)
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN, affiliation not provided to SSRN and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Financial System Resilience and Credit Heterogeneity:,A Comparative Analysis of Consumer Credit and Microfinance in Peru (2004–2025)
detail.abstract: This paper examines how credit heterogeneity shapes financial system resilience in an emerging market context. Using 21 years of monthly data from Peru (2004–2025), I estimate Vector Error Correction (VEC) models and panel data regressions with credit-type fixed effects to document stark differences in cyclical behavior between consumer credit and microfinance. Consumer credit is highly pro-cyclical: GDP elasticity = 1.87 (95% CI: [1.52, 2.22], p < 0.01) and interest-rate semi-elasticity = -0.34 (p < 0.01). Microfinance is essentially counter-cyclical: GDP elasticity = 0.12 (95% CI: [-0.08, 0.32], not significant) and rate sensitivity = -0.08 (not significant). During the three recession episodes in the sample period—the 2008–2009 global financial crisis, the 2014–2016 commodity downturn, and the 2020 pandemic shock—microfinance loan growth remained positive (+8.2%, +6.5%, +5.3% year-over-year) while consumer credit contracted sharply (-12.4%, -8.7%, -15.2%). After 2020, the cointegration trace statistic rose from 42.15 to 58.73, indicating tighter long-run integration despite diverging short-run volatility—a 'cointegration paradox.' Based on these findings, I propose a five-pillar differentiated regulatory framework: segment-specific credit gap indicators, heterogeneous counter-cyclical capital buffer rates, tailored provisioning rules, fiscal–monetary coordination, and institutional safeguards for microfinance institutions. The results have broad applicability across Latin American economies with dual credit structures.

title: Apex Quant: A Multi-Agent Debate Framework For Quantitative Trading

detail.title: Apex Quant: A Multi-Agent Debate Framework For Quantitative Trading
detail.abstract: We present Apex Quant, a multi-agent large language model (LLM) framework for quantitative trading decisions. The system employs three agents with distinct personas-an aggressive bull (Zealot), an aggressive bear (Reaper), and a moderating chief investment officer (Fulcrum)-engaged in structured multi-round debate before reaching a trading decision. Rather than reporting aggregate performance statistics, this paper documents a series of non-obvious architectural discoveries emerging from iterative development and live forward testing: that debate structure itself provides decision stability rather than prompt memory; that systematic persona bias can emerge where one agent consistently dominates through rhetorical structure rather than evidence quality; and that distilling behavioral finance principles directly into agent prompts produces qualitatively superior reasoning compared to relying on base model priors. We describe the full evolution of the system, including failed architectural variants, and present case studies from live forward testing that illustrate both the system's decision mechanisms and the structural tensions inherent in its design, as a practical guide for researchers building LLM-based trading agents.

title: Mortgage risk and inequality during the Covid-19 crisis
affiliations: Bank of Estonia and affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Mortgage risk and inequality during the Covid-19 crisis
detail.abstract: This paper examines how the Covid-19 pandemic reshaped the risk profile of newly issued mortgages and whether its effects differed across income groups. Using quarterly microdata on new housing loans in Estonia from 2018Q1 to 2025Q2, we analyse the evolution of key risk metrics over this period. Two-way fixed effects and quantile regressions are used to identify changes in lending standards and their heterogeneity across borrowers. The results point to a sharp repricing of above-limit mortgages alongside some tightening in lending standards. Banks with lower pre-pandemic exposure to risky lending adjusted more strongly in pricing and risk-taking behaviour. Low-income borrowers did not experience a deterioration in lending conditions, and their share among mortgage borrowers remained stable. Overall, the results provide new micro-level evidence on how borrower-based macroprudential tools interact with large macroeconomic shocks and banks’ risk-taking behaviour.

title: Electricity Prices Beyond the Merit Order: Structural Shocks and Asymmetric Macroeconomic Transmission in Denmark
affiliations: Aalborg University

detail.title: Electricity Prices Beyond the Merit Order: Structural Shocks and Asymmetric Macroeconomic Transmission in Denmark
detail.abstract: This paper investigates the structural drivers of electricity prices and their macroeconomic transmission in Denmark, which has the highest share of wind power in total electricity production among IEA countries. Using a monthly Structural Vector Autoregression (SVAR) over 2000M1-2025M11, we decompose electricity price movements into three distinct shocks: renewable supply (wind-based), natural-gas prices, and aggregate demand. We first assess the relative contribution of each structural shock to electricity price movements, after which we examine how these shocks transmit to core inflation and industrial production. The results indicate that supply-side forces - specifically wind-based electricity generation and natural gas prices - dominate electricity price dynamics, while demand shocks play a modest role. We further test for asymmetry in renewable supply shocks, as implied by the convexity of the merit-order supply curve. We find that renewable supply shocks exhibit pronounced asymmetry: adverse shocks (i.e., reductions in wind-based generation) generate more persistent price increases than the price declines associated with positive shocks. This asymmetry extends beyond electricity price dynamics and generates heterogeneous macroeconomic effects: adverse shocks raise core inflation and depress industrial production, whereas positive shocks, despite lowering electricity prices, do not reduce inflation and only weakly affect industrial production. Historical decompositions suggest that our structural shocks on average account for 68 percent of electricity price fluctuations, with natural gas prices emerging as the main driver of the post-COVID surge in both electricity prices and core inflation. We conclude by discussing the policy implications of these findings for Denmark’s ongoing green transition.

title: Cutting Costs or Cutting Corners: Asset Reallocation in Oil and Gas Production
affiliations: Boston University, University of California, San Diego (UCSD) - Department of Economics and University of Michigan at Ann Arbor

detail.title: Cutting Costs or Cutting Corners: Asset Reallocation in Oil and Gas Production
detail.abstract:
Reallocation of assets across firms can lead to efficiency gains, but it can also lead to distortions via rent-seeking. We examine the link between asset reallocation and rent-seeking enabled by differences in the expected cost of environmental liabilities. Focusing on the US oil and gas industry, we develop a conceptual framework that incorporates both firm specialization in well types and the judgment-proof problem, by which undercapitalized firms can avoid environmental liabilities. We then build a novel dataset with hundreds of thousands of well transfers over 1992 to 2023, showing that oil and gas wells are transferred frequently, particularly as they age and their revenues decline. Moreover, low-value wells are especially likely to be transferred to low-value firms. Transferred wells produce similar amounts in later years, but are less likely to be plugged – thus posing greater environmental risk. We conclude with policy implications related to well plugging, bonding requirements, and decarbonization.

title: Out of the Black Box: Uncertainty Quantification for LLMs via Conditional Probabilities
affiliations: Massachusetts Institute of Technology, University of Melbourne and ESSEC Business School

detail.title: Out of the Black Box: Uncertainty Quantification for LLMs via Conditional Probabilities
detail.abstract:
Autoregressive LLMs generate text by sampling from estimated probability distributions over the next token, conditional on prior context. We use these probabilities to construct an entropy-based measure of prediction uncertainty, termed inner confidence. In news classification, LLM predictions with higher inner confidence are systematically more accurate. To evaluate the measure's economic relevance, we form long-short portfolios based on LLM predictions. The portfolio based on high-confidence predictions achieves a Sharpe ratio about 20\% higher than the unconditional benchmark, while the one based on low-confidence predictions yields no excess returns. In contrast, self-declared confidence exhibits significant decoding biases and provides no comparable performance gains.

title: Words and Bond: Detention Under the Immigration and Nationality Act
affiliations: Roger Williams University School of Law

detail.title: Words and Bond: Detention Under the Immigration and Nationality Act

publicationDetails.detailsText: Roger Williams Univ. Legal Studies Paper No. 226
publicationDetails.journalName: Roger Williams University School of Law Legal Studies Research Paper Series

detail.abstract: Expanded immigration detention has been a pillar of Trump 2.0 policy. Immigration officials are shifting from what this Article calls a tribunal-centered approach, in which an Immigration Judge within the Department of Justice determines bond, to an enforcement-centered approach, in which ICE has the final word, releasing a noncitizen only if it grants a petition for parole. The shift to an enforcement-centered model has ratcheted up the detained population. Trump 2.0 officials have sought to eliminate access to bond for the large number of noncitizens who at any point in recent decades entered the United States surreptitiously, without inspection by immigration officials. In addition, officials have sought to displace ongoing hearings before Immigration Judges, in which noncitizens have a panoply of procedural rights, with the summary process of expedited removal. Officials have also sought to revoke parole, sometimes providing no reasons except for a generic preference for detention. This Article counters that enforcement-centered agenda with a tribunal-centered model that focuses on the text, structure, and history of the Immigration and Nationality Act (INA), along with past practice. Under this model, Immigration Judges should determine whether to release a noncitizen, unless the statutory scheme clearly confers that power on others. Building on recent Supreme Court precedent and established methods of statutory interpretation, the Article shows that Trump 2.0 officials’ view of the INA departs from Congress’s plan.

title: Household Preferences for Women’s Employment: A Field Experiment in Bangladesh
affiliations: University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy, Harvard Business School, University of Chicago - Harris School of Public Policy and University of Chicago

detail.title: Household Preferences for Women’s Employment: A Field Experiment in Bangladesh
detail.abstract:
This paper investigates household preferences over who should work and whether these preferences are malleable. We document that men and women prefer that husbands work over wives. To understand why, we randomly assign a six-week job to either the husband or wife and document asymmetry: women’s work improves their own wellbeing but not their husbands’, while men’s work improves both partners’ wellbeing. One year later, we surprise households with a work opportunity. Both women and men in households where women were previously employed are more likely to prefer the woman take the job and express fewer concerns about women’s employment in general.

title: Life Cycle Portfolio Choice with Human Capital and Social Security
affiliations: Independent, Stanford University - Department of Economics, George Mason University - School of Policy, Government, and International Affairs and Stanford Graduate School of Business

detail.title: Life Cycle Portfolio Choice with Human Capital and Social Security
detail.abstract:
Target date funds – which initially invest a large share of retirement savings in stocks and shift gradually towards bonds over the life cycle – are designed to provide a “one stop shop” for retirement investing. The rationale for this pattern is that human capital, which is highest at the start of a worker’s career, is “bond-like.” Thus, utility is maximized when financial wealth is initially invested primarily in stocks, with the investment mix shifting towards bonds as the present value of future labor income declines. We revisit this logic in a dynamic model in which shocks to labor income are correlated with the stock market, and in which Social Security replaces a higher share of income for lower-income individuals. In line with empirical evidence, lower-income individuals in the model experience a higher degree of correlation between labor earnings growth and stock returns. We find that utility-maximizing retirement portfolios can vary greatly across individuals, deviating substantially from the pattern of a target date fund for lower-income individuals.

title: The Global Incumbency Advantage
affiliations: , Boston University, Harvard University - Business School (HBS) and Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT)

detail.title: The Global Incumbency Advantage
detail.abstract:
This paper explores the global incumbency advantage. We first show that existing subnational estimates of the incumbency advantage correlate positively with GDP per capita and democratic quality, and negatively with corruption across countries. Building on this meta-analysis, we then consider all presidential and parliamentary elections held since 1945 to estimate how a national electoral victory affects the probability that winning parties and candidates retain power beyond the term for which they were elected. On average, national election winners benefit from an incumbency advantage, but this effect is short-lived and differs markedly across contexts: it is large in Africa, North America, and Western Europe, but muted or even reversed in other regions. We explore how standard incumbency effects and electoral manipulation contribute to these results. In established democracies, the national incumbency advantage reflects gains in the subsequent electoral performance of election winners. In less democratic regimes, it mainly stems from manipulation of the fairness and the timing of elections. Overall, this advantage is largest in both the most and the least democratic countries, due to radically different types of equilibria.

title: Mutual Party Extremism
affiliations: University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA)

detail.title: Mutual Party Extremism
detail.abstract:
With four political candidates competing first in two primaries and then in a general election, even a modestly polarized electorate can sustain (in equilibrium) much more extremist candidates. However, a party can sustain extremism only if the other side is extreme, too. A small moderation of one side’s voting electorate can trigger a discontinuous collapse of candidate extremism on both sides — a “moderation export” effect. The converse is also true: minute increases in voter polarization on the more moderate side can trigger radical candidate extremism on both sides. Principled candidates can destroy party electability. Distance-related voter abstention favors extremism.

title: The max EPS Paradigm for Corporate Finance
affiliations: National Bureau of Economic Research (NBER) and Michigan State University - Eli Broad College of Business

detail.title: The max EPS Paradigm for Corporate Finance
detail.abstract:
There are three classic problems in corporate finance: capital structure, real investment, and payout policy. In three companion papers, we characterize the max EPS solution to each one. The max EPS approach delivers an optimal leverage ratio even in the absence of frictions, an investment rule based on comparing yields rather than using a risk-adjusted discount rate, and a payout policy where accretive buybacks are preferred to neutral dividends. Our max EPS model draws a bright line between growth and value. Growth stocks have earnings yields below the riskfree rate; value stocks have earnings yields above it. This single comparison leads the two kinds of firms to pursue different constellations of EPS-maximizing policies. The model also produces easy-to-follow calculations that closely mirror what practitioners actually do. This review article ties together these results to form a new max EPS paradigm for corporate-finance research.

title: Loaded Chambers: Organized Interests, Public Opinion, and Policy Responsiveness in the American States
affiliations: Stanford University, Stanford University, Stanford Law School and Stanford University

detail.title: Loaded Chambers: Organized Interests, Public Opinion, and Policy Responsiveness in the American States
detail.abstract:
Organized interests are thought to influence policy, but whether and when interest group money overrides public opinion remains poorly understood. We investigate how gun interest group money and public opinion shape state gun laws. To test which force drives policy, we link 25 years of campaign finance records to a novel Gun Law Index paired with original estimates of constituent sentiment, 2000--2024. We show that pro-gun contributions produce deregulatory changes under Republican trifectas, while gun safety contributions generate regulatory tightening under Democratic trifectas. Using an instrumental variable design, we find that constituent sentiment does not causally predict policy change under Republican or Democratic trifectas. We document one of the most striking failures of democratic responsiveness in the history of the American Republic: while the twelve states in which universal background checks command at least 90% support have adopted them, only 8 other states have done so among the 36 states that have support between 80-90%, while assault weapons bans and concealed carry restrictions also enjoy durable majority support across 36 states, yet there has been far greater deregulation than regulation for both measures. These patterns provide unequivocal evidence that organized interests, rather than constituent preferences, drive gun policy in the United States.

detail.abstract: Standard economic theory predicts that populations stripped of physical, financial, institutional, and social capital should remain trapped in persistent poverty. Yet empirical evidence from post-genocide and post-conflict diasporas reveals a striking anomaly: certain displaced communities achieve remarkable economic trajectories despite near-total capital destruction. This paper introduces the concept of Phoenix Capital, defined as a latent and transmissible form of capital that survives systemic destruction and enables economic regeneration. I propose that Phoenix Capital comprises three components: Productive Memory (tacit knowledge and dormant networks), Existential Debt (the felt obligation to succeed for those who did not survive), and Identity Arbitrage (the capacity to navigate multiple cultural and economic systems). Drawing on the Tamil Eelam diaspora as an empirical foundation, I develop a theoretical framework demonstrating the distinctive properties of Phoenix Capital: antifragility under destruction, non-linear intergenerational transmission, and increasing returns under specific institutional conditions. This framework establishes the foundation for a new research paradigm I term Phoenixnomics, offering analytical tools for understanding refugee economics, climate displacement, and post-crisis reconstruction. In an era of unprecedented global displacement, this framework provides both rigorous analysis and a humanist vision: that beyond our divisions of race, religion, caste, and ideology lies a shared capacity for renewal that defines our common humanity.

title: How LLMs Reshape Equilibrium: A Study of Human-AI Competition in Auctions
affiliations: , Southwest Jiaotong University, University of International Business and Economics and Tsinghua University

detail.title: How LLMs Reshape Equilibrium: A Study of Human-AI Competition in Auctions
detail.abstract: With the rapid development of AI technologies, LLM agents are increasingly deployed as autonomous decision-makers in economic contexts, rather than merely as advisory tools. This shift fosters human-AI synthetic environments, in which human decision-makers interact and compete with LLM agents. Economists have developed an equilibrium framework to understand and predict human strategies and to guide mechanism design. However, whether this equilibrium framework continues to apply in human-AI synthetic competitive environments remains an open question. To this end, we conduct a series of common-value auction experiments, in which simulation agents and equilibrium agents are used to model human bidders interacting with LLM agents. Using descriptive comparisons and mixed-effects model analyses, we find that LLM agents' bidding strategies (ChatGPT and DeepSeek) exhibit systematic deviations from equilibrium bidding. At high-valuation levels, aggressive bids lead LLM agents to suffer from the winner's curse, despite some degree of bid shading. In contrast, both LLM agents exhibit limited sensitivity to underestimation at low-valuation levels. Further, learning effect from historical outcome feedback can mitigate the severity of the winner's curse. Importantly, when facing LLM opponents, Nash equilibrium strategies may no longer constitute optimal responses, particularly when LLM agents adopt aggressive bidding strategies. Moreover, auction scale and valuation uncertainty further undermine the optimality of equilibrium. These findings also suggest that organizers may need to move beyond mechanism design approaches based solely on equilibrium predictions.

title: Decomposing Alpha in a Machine-Learning Gold Timing System: Trend Following, Forecast Quality, and the Cost of Look-Ahead Bias
affiliations: and

detail.title: Decomposing Alpha in a Machine-Learning Gold Timing System: Trend Following, Forecast Quality, and the Cost of Look-Ahead Bias

declarations.declarationOfInterest: The authors declare no conflicts of interest. The research was conducted independently and without financial relationships that could be perceived as influencing the results.
declarations.funderStatement: This research received no external funding and was conducted independently by the authors.

detail.abstract: A systematic audit of a four-layer gold timing system reveals that training label leakage, a subtle form of look-ahead bias in walk-forward backtests inflated the ML forecast’s apparent quality from insignificant (IC = 0.08, p = 0.25) to seemingly significant (IC = 0.23, p = 0.001). Correcting the leak reduced the system’s Sharpe ratio from 1.01 to 0.91. The mechanism is general: when forecast targets reference prices beyond the prediction date, the last H training rows borrow signal from the future. A 21-day embargo and a 3-day COT release lag correction restore honest performance; less than 2% of training data was leaked, but it produced 65% of the apparent forecast signal. With the leak corrected, we decompose the alpha of the system’s four layers, a conventional golden cross filter, GMM regime detection, a four-model supervised ensemble (Ridge and Gradient Boosting), and volatility-targeted sizing over 2010–2026. The trend filter provides the structural foundation: it contributes modest Sharpe improvement (+0.036) but dominates risk reduction, compressing maximum drawdown from −44.6% to −32.8%. The regime detection and forecasting ensemble adds a further 0.21 Sharpe (from 0.70 to 0.91), but this improvement is not statistically significant: the Ledoit-Wolf test cannot reject equality between the full system and the golden-cross-with-vol-targeting Sharpe (p = 0.20), and a random exit null model places the production system between the 74th and 98th percentile depending on whether the null samples from all golden cross days or only near activation dates (p = 0.01–0.26). A simple trailing stop within the golden cross regime achieves Sharpe 0.69 with zero ML infrastructure, capturing 76% of the full system’s performance. Volatility targeting contributes essentially nothing (+0.001 Sharpe). Performance is concentrated, three trades account for 82% of returns and the first-half Sharpe (2010–2017) is 0.44, suggesting the full-period figure depends substantially on the 2024 to 2026 gold rally. The honest conclusion is that the system’s alpha is structural (trend following) rather than predictive (ML forecasting). These findings demonstrate that layer-by-layer decomposition, null model testing, and training data auditing are essential before attributing performance to complex components and that the most valuable discovery in a trading system may be what does not work.

title: Behavioral Recognition Technology
affiliations: Bar-Ilan University - Faculty of Law, Bar-Ilan University - Faculty of Law and University of San Diego School of Law

detail.title: Behavioral Recognition Technology

publicationDetails.journalName: University of San Diego Law School Legal Studies Research Paper Series

publicationDetails.detailsText: Bar Ilan University Faculty of Law Research Paper (forthcoming)
publicationDetails.journalName: Bar-Ilan University Public Law & Legal Theory Research Paper Series

detail.abstract:
The rapid adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) by regulatory agencies marks a fundamental shift in legal compliance and enforcement. While law and policy debates have heatedly focused on the threat of AI biometric tools such as facial recognition technology (FRT) to privacy and equality, the field of AI-driven behavioral recognition technology (BRT) has been far less charted. In contrast to FRT, BRT uses machine learning not simply to identify who a person is but to predict what they are likely to do. Agencies from the IRS to the EPA increasingly deploy these algorithmic tools to predict individual and corporate behavior and the likelihood of regulatory violations, yet legal scholarship has focused more narrowly on government use of AI in policing and criminal law enforcement. This Article demonstrates that as governments and administrative agencies embrace BRT to make fine-grained determinations about whom to trust and whom to monitor, investigate, audit, or sanction—and in turn to determine how to allocate limited enforcement resources—behavioral prediction becomes a central technology of governance.

In providing the first comprehensive legal framework for evaluating and ethically implementing BRT, this Article makes three key contributions. First, it maps how regulatory agencies are using AI-driven technology to make nuanced determinations about whom to trust and monitor, revealing an emerging regulatory paradigm that accelerates a paradigm shift from traditional command-and-control approaches toward data-driven trust assessments. Second, it argues that while deploying BRT as a regulatory practice raises significant constitutional and administrative law concerns regarding privacy, equality, and autonomy, properly designed systems can enhance these values by enabling more individualized and evidence-based enforcement decisions, as opposed to random selection or demographic-based proxies. Third, it develops a novel normative blueprint for responsible deployment of BRT in regulatory enforcement. The Article establishes a set of principles including the privileging of individual over group-based predictions, requiring strong empirical justification for public sector cross-domain data use, and dynamic balancing of predictive accuracy with civil rights protection. Rather than embracing or rejecting BRT wholesale, as has too often been the case with debates and policies on FRT, we chart a dynamic path forward that harnesses these tools’ benefits while preserving democratic values and individual rights. The Article concludes by offering practical guidance for courts and agencies evaluating and implementing these emerging technologies.

title: Antitrust & Gig Workers: Labor Exemption as Protection
affiliations: Seton Hall Law School

detail.abstract: If applicable, the labor exemption to antitrust law serves to improve the welfare of gig workers by empowering them to engage in collective bargaining without fear of antitrust liability. The exemption, however, has long been construed to benefit only employees, not independent contractors, and gig workers are usually classified as independent contractors. While the First Circuit recently deviated from this standard interpretation in the “Jockeys” case, it is too soon to know whether that case will ultimately transform the exemption or be treated as an outlier. Tracing the historical evolution of the labor exemption and the Norris-LaGuardia Act, and drawing on case law, I contend that while doctrinal reliance on the employee-independent contractor distinction might have had logic initially, it has become ill-suited to modern labor markets dominated by platform intermediation. Given the human values expressed in the statutory language of the labor exemption and the Norris-LaGuardia Act, a compelling case can be made for repositioning the labor exemption as a tool for worker empowerment in the platform economy.

title: Advances in Communication Technology and the Marriage Market: A Non-stationary Two-sided Search Model

detail.title: Advances in Communication Technology and the Marriage Market: A Non-stationary Two-sided Search Model
detail.abstract: Do advances in communication technology change the value of being in a relationship? I develop a non-stationary two-sided search equilibrium model with cohabitation to quantify their effects on marital behavior and welfare. The models equilibrium conditions provide a new identification strategy that separates mating preferences from matching technology. I estimate the model by indirect inference using the NLS 72 and NLSY 97 cohort data. The results show that changes in mating preferences, rather than advances in communication technology itself, are the primary drivers of observed changes in marital behavior and the value of being matched.

publicationDetails.detailsText: Ca' Foscari University of Venice, Department of Economics Research Paper Series No. 09/2026

detail.abstract: Climate shelters contribute to heat resilience directly, as cool spaces, and indirectly, as community venues for information provision. In a 2025 pilot project in Venice, Italy, we analyse, through surveys and interviews, four possible bottlenecks to shelter use: heat risk perception, awareness of shelters, accessibility, and motivation. We test, through a treatment-control experiment, the impact of information provision in shelters. We find that awareness of shelters is the easiest bottleneck to address. Accessibility hinges on funding and governance constraints. Motivation is context and place driven: green, outdoor, spaces are the most popular, but less well prepared. Risk perception is a crucial policy target, since it drives use and adoption of protective behaviours. Yet, it is sticky: individuals, particularly the elderly, underestimate risk. Information provision did not change risk perception. It, however, increased awareness of shelters and adaptation knowledge. Peer effects and seamless integration of events within community centers promote effectiveness.

title: Measuring Spousal Cooperation: A Biform Game Approach to Intra-Household Allocation

detail.title: Measuring Spousal Cooperation: A Biform Game Approach to Intra-Household Allocation
detail.abstract: Do households cooperate or not? Existing models force a binary choice between full cooperation and non-cooperation, yet reality likely lies in between. I develop an empirical biform game framework that identifies the degree of spousal cooperation from data. The model treats enforceable decisions (labor supply) cooperatively and non-enforceable decisions (childcare) non-cooperatively, with a caring parameter nesting both extremes. Equilibrium uniqueness and monotonicity properties deliver a novel identification strategy: the cooperation parameter is identified from slope moments-how childcare responds to wages and labor supply-rather than level moments. Applying the framework to households with disabled children, I find 33% lower cooperation, reduced paternal childcare efficiency, and shifted happiness benchmarks. Counterfactual analysis shows that even large Child SSI increases cannot realistically close the welfare gap. This highlights the fundamental limits of cash transfers and the importance of policies supporting spousal cooperation.

detail.abstract: This working paper presents new evidence suggesting that India misestimated its annual growth rate during the past two decades. Growth during the boom years between 2005 and 2011 may have been underestimated by about 1-1½ percentage points on average; and subsequent growth between 2012 and 2023 may have been overestimated by about 1½-2 percentage points. Once these adjustments are made, it appears that the Indian economy did not grow at a stable rate over the past two decades but rather boomed during the early 2000s, then decelerated after the global financial crisis and subsequent domestic shocks. The misestimation problem can be traced to two methodological issues. The first is that the formal sector has been used as a proxy for the vast informal sector, even though unorganized enterprises were disproportionately hit after 2015 by demonetization, the introduction of the goods and services tax, and the COVID-19 pandemic. The second is that deflators for many sectors have been based on commodity prices, which have moved sharply in relative terms. The methodological revisions in February 2026, made following commendable consultations, aim to address the challenges identified.

title: Insolvency Without Predictability? A Computational Census of 4,820 IBC Cases and the Information Asymmetry Problem

detail.title: Insolvency Without Predictability? A Computational Census of 4,820 IBC Cases and the Information Asymmetry Problem
detail.abstract: India's net Foreign Direct Investment collapsed from $10 billion to $353 million in FY2024-25. Foreign investors consistently cite regulatory uncertainty and insolvency framework unpredictability among their concerns. The conventional diagnosis attributes this to judicial arbitrariness in IBC proceedings-the perception that outcomes depend more on bench assignment than case merits. This paper examines that diagnosis using computational analysis of the complete corpus of resolved insolvency proceedings in India. The dataset of 4,820 cases represents approximately 100% of "meaningful closures" reported by the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Board of India through September 2024, making this a census rather than a sample. Using Graph Convolutional Networks, the analysis finds that IBC outcomes are 71.9% predictable from observable case characteristics-creditor composition, Committee of Creditors dynamics, promoter behavior, and sector. This finding is inconsistent with the arbitrariness hypothesis: if outcomes were truly random, predictability would approach the 35.9% majority-class baseline. The paper suggests that the underlying problem may not be judicial inconsistency but information asymmetry. Sophisticated institutional players-PSU banks, Asset Reconstruction Companies, distressed debt funds-may be able to discern these patterns. Smaller creditors and foreign investors without local expertise perceive chaos where structure exists. Monte Carlo counterfactual analysis indicates that scenario modeling (e.g., "what if the promoter cooperates?") shifts outcome probabilities by 60-70 percentage points-analysis available to sophisticated players but opaque to others. The paper proposes expanding Information Utilities under Section 214-215 of the IBC to democratize predictive insights, potentially restoring investor confidence in India's insolvency framework.

This qualitative study investigates the critical intersection of technology adoption and long-term business sustainability within the Cape Town printing industry. Amidst a significant shift from traditional to digital processes, the research utilizes thematic analysis of data gathered from diverse industry stakeholders—including executive directors and production managers—to identify the impact of digital printing, cloud-based solutions, and automation on operational efficiency.

The findings reveal that while technological advancements significantly enhance customer satisfaction and cost-saving measures, substantial barriers such as high capital requirements and workforce upskilling remains. The study provides a strategic framework for SMEs to navigate digital transformation, emphasizing that long-term sustainability requires a transition from purely transactional equipment acquisition to integrated, technology-driven strategic planning.

title: Creating Shareholder Value for Companies Sponsoring Football Clubs: Market Reaction to Match Days in UEFA Competitions 2024/2025

detail.title: Creating Shareholder Value for Companies Sponsoring Football Clubs: Market Reaction to Match Days in UEFA Competitions 2024/2025
detail.abstract: This study examines whether matchdays in the new UEFA competition format for the 2024/2025 season are associated with a short-term market premium for shareholders of publicly listed companies sponsoring football clubs through brand and logo exposure on jerseys. An event-study approach was used; expected rates of return were determined based on the Fama-French five-factor model, followed by calculation of daily excess returns and their cumulative values in event windows surrounding the match day. In the main event window [0;1], the average cumulative effect is positive, while the daily profile indicates a concentration of market reactions on the match day. Positive results also persist in the alternative event window [-1;1], confirming the stability of the observed effect in the short term. Cross-sectional analyses in the [0;1] window show positive cumulative returns for all match outcomes and positive effects across all competition types, with the strongest significance for the Europa League. Regarding the competition phase, the most stable effect is observed in the league phase. The results are consistent with the assumption that short-term investor attention and event visibility play a key role, with the bulk of the price reaction concentrated in the immediate matchday environment.

title: Time-Varying Factor Exposure of Silver as a Hybrid Asset and Its Implications for Dynamic Asset Allocation

detail.title: Time-Varying Factor Exposure of Silver as a Hybrid Asset and Its Implications for Dynamic Asset Allocation

detail.abstract:
Silver has traditionally been classified as either a precious metal or an industrial commodity. However, silver simultaneously exhibits monetary characteristics and industrial demand properties, suggesting that its economic role may evolve over time. From this perspective, this study empirically investigates the time-varying factor exposure of silver and examines the effectiveness of a dynamic asset exposure management strategy that exploits such structural changes.

Using daily ETF data from 2012 to 2026, rolling regression analysis and structural break tests reveal that the price determination mechanism of silver is not stable over time. In particular, the relative influence of industrial commodity factors has strengthened since 2020. To quantify this structural transition, this study constructs an Industrial Tilt indicator based on the differential sensitivity between copper and gold factor exposures.

Based on this indicator, a Hybrid Dynamic strategy that conditionally adjusts silver allocation is implemented. The empirical results show that the proposed strategy delivers moderate but consistently positive risk-adjusted excess returns compared to static asset allocation portfolios with equivalent average risk exposure. Statistical testing using Newey–West HAC standard errors confirms significance at the 10% level, and transaction cost sensitivity analysis further indicates that the strategy retains economic viability under realistic investment conditions.

The findings suggest that asset allocation performance depends not only on asset selection itself but also on dynamic exposure management responding to changes in the underlying economic characteristics of assets. This study contributes to the literature by interpreting silver as a hybrid asset with time-varying factor structure and by linking structural asset characteristics to practical portfolio decision-making.

title: Currencies That Discount Lives: Coercion, Monetary Hierarchy, and Extraction in the International System

detail.title: Currencies That Discount Lives: Coercion, Monetary Hierarchy, and Extraction in the International System
detail.abstract: Why does one currency matter more than another in the global economy? Conventional explanations point to productivity, institutions, or the depth and liquidity of financial markets; Modern Monetary Theory (MMT) emphasizes the state's ability to impose a unit of account through taxation. This article advances a sharper proposition: international monetary supremacy is anchored, in the last instance, by enforceable power beyond borders-the credible capacity to impose consequences through military reach, sanctions, and control over critical financial infrastructure. Markets and institutions are not dismissed; they are treated as amplifiers that operationalize supremacy at scale. Building on this premise, the article frames monetary hegemony as a mechanism of extraction: the hegemon can exchange its liabilities (currency and sovereign debt) for real goods, labor, and strategic resources produced elsewhere, thereby discounting foreign futures into present command over life and material production. A compact system of differential equations formalizes the self-reinforcing loop among coercive capacity, network lock-in, safe-asset demand, and net real-resource absorption. Historical vignettes-from sterling and gold-era discipline to Bretton Woods, the 1971 break, petrodollar-era recycling, and SWIFT-era sanctions-illustrate how monetary order tracks power, and how "neutral" finance can function as a quietly violent architecture of valuation.

title: Beyond the Linear Dream: Why Medicine Must Awaken from the RCT Paradigm -and Where Science Should Go Next

detail.abstract:
For more than half a century, the randomized controlled trial (RCT) has occupied the apex of medicine's evidence hierarchy. This position rests on a set of assumptions — that interventions act linearly, that populations can be meaningfully averaged, that time is exchangeable, and that the response of a heterogeneous individual can be predicted from the mean response of a homogeneous sample — which are the assumptions of equilibrium physics, not of living systems.

We argue that this mismatch is not a statistical problem but a physical one. Living organisms are dissipative structures operating far from thermodynamic equilibrium. Their pathological states, particularly in chronic disease, may involve phase transitions: discontinuous, hysteretic, irreversible changes in the physical state of the interstitial medium that cannot be captured by linear, additive experimental designs. The RCT is the right tool for the wrong ontology.

But our argument does not stop at critique. We propose a positive vision for post-linear medicine, grounded in five principles: the replacement of state-measurement with process-measurement; the abandonment of population homogeneity in favor of individual trajectories; the adoption of convergent validity across heterogeneous methods; the integration of thermodynamic state variables into clinical assessment; and the reorientation of medical intervention from molecular targeting to thermodynamic field restoration. This is not a call to abandon rigor. It is a call to apply rigor to the right kind of system.

title: Property, Power, and the Corporate Form: A Hybrid Theory of UK Company Law

detail.title: Property, Power, and the Corporate Form: A Hybrid Theory of UK Company Law
detail.abstract: This article reconstructs the theoretical foundations of UK company law through a hybrid framework integrating property theory, agency theory, managerialism, and the political economy of the ownership society. It argues that the corporate form is best understood as a property-structured governance architecture in which the company holds title to assets, directors exercise control as fiduciaries, and shareholders retain residual governance rights. This allocation of proprietary and control rights explains the structure of directors' duties, the limits of enlightened shareholder value, and the persistence of shareholder primacy. The analysis traces the evolution of the corporation from state-chartered institution to managerial enterprise to financialised investment vehicle, showing how these transformations shaped the modern governance framework. It concludes that meaningful reform requires confronting the corporation's dual character as both a property-holding institution and a public-impact entity, and re-evaluating the corporate objective accordingly.

title: Fixed and Floating Charges Over Book Debts: Restoring Legal and Commercial Certainty

detail.title: Fixed and Floating Charges Over Book Debts: Restoring Legal and Commercial Certainty
detail.abstract: The case law surrounding fixed and floating charges over book debts has become unnecessarily complex, generating legal uncertainty and undermining commercial confidence. This analysis resolves the post-Spectrum Plus uncertainty by demonstrating that proprietary attachment via trust (not account control) determines fixed charge status. This paper argues that much of this confusion stems from a departure from the doctrinal architecture established in Holroyd v Marshall¹ and reinforced by the Law of Property Act 1925,² the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989,³ and modern trust jurisprudence. By returning to this legal framework, we can restore clarity to the creation of fixed charges, the nature of floating charges, the role of trusts, and the irrelevance of "blocked accounts" as a proprietary test. This paper also acknowledges the Lexology analysis, 'Fixed or floating charge? The importance of control',⁴ as a key source of insight in clarifying the doctrinal errors surrounding blocked accounts.

title: Restoring Commercial Certainty: Fixed Charges, Floating Charges, and the Restoration of Holroyd -Why Control Is Evidential, Not Constitutive

detail.title: Restoring Commercial Certainty: Fixed Charges, Floating Charges, and the Restoration of Holroyd -Why Control Is Evidential, Not Constitutive
detail.abstract: This paper challenges the modern orthodoxy that a fixed charge over book debts requires the creditor to exercise operational control over the debtor's bank accounts. That orthodoxy, rooted in Re Spectrum Plus Ltd and Agnew v Commissioner of Inland Revenue (Re Brumark Investments Ltd), has obscured the doctrinal foundation of English security law. Drawing on Holroyd v Marshall, the Law of Property Act 1925, the Law of Property (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act 1989, National Provincial Bank v Ainsworth, Saunders v Vautier, and Re Lehman Brothers International (Europe), this paper demonstrates that a fixed charge arises through equitable attachment and trust, not through blocked accounts or segregation. Once a book debt comes into existence, the mortgagee acquires a vested equitable proprietary interest, and the mortgagor holds the legal title as trustee. By contrast, a floating charge is non-proprietary until crystallisation. The paper concludes that the blocked-account doctrine is a misinterpretation: control is evidential rather than constitutive, and commercial certainty is restored when the law returns to its equitable foundations.

title: The Effectiveness of Fuel Treatments on Moderating Early Wildfire Spread

detail.title: The Effectiveness of Fuel Treatments on Moderating Early Wildfire Spread
detail.abstract: The state of Oregon experienced an unprecedented wildfire event during the summer of 2020. Historically extreme weather led to the ignition of over 500 recorded wildfires across the state between August 15 and September 8, the majority of which remained small. Twenty-four of these ignitions escaped containment and became large, destructive megafires exceeding 1,000 acres. This paper investigates why, during a stress test of the entire forest system, only 5% of ignitions escaped containment. Using a novel dataset of all fire ignitions on National Forest lands, we employ a series of parametric and non-parametric approaches to disentangle the effect of previous fuel treatments on the probability of a fire escaping containment. Logistic regressions show that severe weather was a driving factor in the event, with probability of escape being highly associated with extreme aridity and high wind gusts in the hours following ignition. The random forest, which allows for flexible, non-linear interactions between variables, uncovers previous prescribed fire treatment as the most consistent and durable predictor of contained fires. Our findings demonstrate that even under extreme weather-driven conditions, proactive fuel management can moderate the behavior of fires and play an important role in preventing future megafires.

detail.abstract: This study examines the dual reality of Yemen's education system following a decade of protracted conflict: its profound systemic collapse and the emergent, grassroots potential within it to serve as a catalyst for peacebuilding and gender equality. Employing a qualitative multi-site case study design grounded in political economy and feminist analysis, this research synthesizes data from 45 semi-structured interviews with Yemeni educators, community leaders, and education actors across five governorates (Aden, Taiz, Hadramawt, Marib, and Sana'a), complemented by analysis of international reports and peer-reviewed scholarship. The findings reveal a landscape where institutional destruction, teacher precarity, and gendered exclusion are pervasive-with 3.1 million children out of school, only 30% of teachers receiving regular salaries, and secondary school gender parity at 0.50. However, within this landscape, community-based schools, women-led educational projects, and adaptive learning models demonstrate tangible potential to foster social cohesion and advance women's agency. The analysis applies the "4Rs" framework (Redistribution, Recognition, Representation, Reconciliation) to assess these emergent practices, revealing both their contributions and limitations. A forward-looking scenario model projects trajectories under conditions of stagnation, fragmentation, or managed stability, with early warning indicators for adaptive planning. The study concludes that leveraging this potential requires a fundamental paradigm shift-from treating education as a short-term humanitarian service to investing in it as a long-term, strategic pillar of inclusive peacebuilding. This entails contextspecific, politically-informed support for locally-owned initiatives, curriculum reform, and guaranteed support for teachers, with sustained commitment to gender-transformative practices.

detail.abstract: Bathing soap has evolved from a rudimentary mixture of fat and ash into a technologically sophisticated personal care product shaped by chemistry, industrialization, dermatology, public health, and consumer behaviour. This paper synthesizes historical records, chemical science, dermatological research, industrial development, and market dynamics to examine the transformation of soap from a cleansing agent to a science-driven global industry. detail.title: The Vanishing Wage Effect: Immigration, Task Prices, and Endogenous College Major Choice in General Equilibrium
detail.abstract: We develop and estimate a dynamic general equilibrium model in which forward-looking students choose college majors in response to immigration-induced task price movements. Our framework closes the loop between immigrant labor supply, education decisions, and future native wages. We show that endogenous native reallocation not only offsets but more than fully reverses the partial-equilibrium wage effect of immigration, generating long-run wage responses that differ sharply from static estimates. The overshooting reflects substantial task complementarity, which amplifies education reallocation relative to the direct wage channel. A leave-one-task-out decomposition reveals that the adjustment is driven entirely by divergence between interpersonal and IT task prices, a dimension absent from standard cognitive/manual frameworks.

title: Negotiating Coordination: A Study in Retail Gasoline
affiliations: University of Melbourne, University of Liverpool, Clemson University - John E. Walker Department of Economics, Duke University - Fuqua School of Business, Economics Group and University of Melbourne

detail.title: Negotiating Coordination: A Study in Retail Gasoline
detail.abstract: We examine a unique five-year equilibrium transition in the retail gasoline industry using hourly station-level price data. In an attempt to increase profit margins under a focal pricing structure, price leaders alter asymmetrically sized retailers' incentives to coordinate on prices, spurring bargaining over transfers that support coordination. Such bargaining occurs in near real-time through platform-enabled, price-based communication under strategic uncertainty. After three turbulent years of bargaining without resolution, which entail multiple price wars and experimentation that enable firms to reveal their pricing strategies and learn rivals', price leaders gradually adapt to a new price-signaling structure that ultimately yields stable, shared long-run profit growth. We discuss implications for the theory of collusion and for antitrust policies aimed at limiting the anticompetitive effects of digital information-sharing and pricing algorithms.

title: Marketing Scholarship and Environmentally-Sustainable Retailing: A Two-Stage Framework for Greener Consumption and Production

detail.title: Marketing Scholarship and Environmentally-Sustainable Retailing: A Two-Stage Framework for Greener Consumption and Production
detail.abstract: Marketing scholarship in the retailing domain can play an important role in advancing environmentally sustainable consumption and production. We synthesize prior research across marketing and related fields and introduce a novel two-stage framework that examines sustainability interventions through the lens of retail-actor interactions. The framework characterizes how different actors (e.g., consumers, retailers, manufacturers, regulators) influence one another and evaluates interventions in terms of feasibility and environmental impact. Although marketing has contributed to unsustainable consumption patterns, we argue that it holds significant potential to accelerate the transition toward environmental sustainability. Retail emerges not only as a context in which sustainability challenges manifest, but as a strategic domain where coordinated action can drive transformative change. Our framework offers a structured approach to mapping interventions, assessing their effectiveness, and understanding the mechanisms that link the interventions to their effectiveness. It helps stakeholders identify the most promising strategies to foster environmentally sustainable behavior and manage interactions across the retail ecosystem. The framework informs marketing scholars by highlighting research gaps, by revealing barriers that limit the effectiveness of current interventions, and by pointing to opportunities to adapt successful approaches across actors to better support sustainability goals.

The findings demonstrate that developing repatronage intentions, word-of-mouth recommendations, and willingness to pay more can be facilitated through experience quality and satisfaction. Also, it is proved that satisfaction is positively influenced by destination image. Moreover, authenticity and involvement positively influence destination image. According to research results, to increase willingness to pay, it is imperative to offer a high-quality cultural tourism experience, wherein tourists gain knowledge about the heritage destination and enjoy the experience while deeply engaging with the surroundings. Furthermore, public and private organisations should design visitor experiences that consider authenticity and involvement to enhance destination image and increase customer satisfaction.

title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Personalized Marketing: Consumer Attitudes and Purchase Intention
affiliations: Rajamangala University of Technology Krungthep and Rajamangala University of Technology Krungthep

detail.title: Artificial Intelligence-Driven Personalized Marketing: Consumer Attitudes and Purchase Intention
detail.abstract: The growing integration of artificial intelligence into contemporary marketing practices has fundamentally altered the manner in which organizations communicate with consumers. AI technologies equip marketers with the capacity to process substantial volumes of consumer data, automate complex decision-making processes, and deliver highly tailored communications at scale. Nevertheless, despite the accelerating pace of AI adoption across marketing functions, significant questions persist regarding how consumers evaluate, trust, and ultimately respond to AI-generated marketing content. This paper reviews and critically discusses recent scholarly literature published within the last five years, with a particular focus on the intersection of AI-driven personalized marketing, consumer psychological responses, and purchase intention. Drawing upon the Theory of Planned Behavior and the Diffusion of Innovation Theory as interpretive lenses, the discussion explores the mechanisms through which AI marketing shapes consumer decision-making. The weight of available evidence points toward consumer attitude functioning as a pivotal mediating variable connecting AI-driven marketing practices to purchase intention, with trust, perceived value, compatibility, transparency, and privacy concerns each exerting meaningful influence over consumer acceptance. The paper further reflects on existing gaps in the literature and offers commentary on productive directions for future inquiry that would support ethical and sustainable AI marketing practice.

title: UEFA Matches as Information-Driven Value-Creating Events: Abnormal Stock Returns of Main Sponsors of Football Clubs in the 2024/2025 Season

detail.title: UEFA Matches as Information-Driven Value-Creating Events: Abnormal Stock Returns of Main Sponsors of Football Clubs in the 2024/2025 Season
detail.abstract: This paper examines the short-term capital market response to match days of clubs participating in UEFA competitions in the 2024/2025 season from the perspective of publicly listed firms acting as clubs' main sponsors (e.g., shirt-front sponsors). An event-study framework is applied; expected returns are estimated separately for each firm using the Fama-French five-factor model with an estimation window of [-250;-30]. The sample comprises 281 events. The average abnormal return equals approximately 0.40% on the match day and 0.27% on the first trading day after the match. Cumulative average abnormal returns reach 0.67% in the [0;1] window, 0.85% in [-1;1], and 0.95% in [-2;3]. A positive effect is observed for both home and away matches. Next, a cross-sectional regression is estimated for cumulative abnormal returns in the [0;1] window, testing the influence of selected match-related variables (stadium attendance, venue, and goal difference). The regression results do not indicate statistically significant determinants, suggesting that the market prices the sponsor's exposure around match day itself, whereas heterogeneity across matches may require additional measures capturing sporting and media-information context.

title: Telemedicine apps and their Influence on the Tourism Industry. A Qualitative Study
affiliations: Universidad Complutense Madrid and

detail.title: Telemedicine apps and their Influence on the Tourism Industry. A Qualitative Study
detail.abstract:
Purpose: Despite increasing interest in telemedicine, its impact on tourism remains underexplored. This study analyses how telemedicine apps improve healthcare access for tourists, emphasizing usability, benefits, challenges, and safety perceptions, while identifying integration barriers and opportunities. 

Design/methodology/approach: This study employs a qualitative approach using Grounded Theory to develop a structured understanding of telemedicine's role in tourism. Data collection involved semi-structured in-depth interviews, participant observation, and document review with 10 experts from medicine, tourism, app development, consumer advocacy, and academia, recruited through theoretical sampling. The analysis employed ATLAS.ti software with open, axial, and selective coding to generate themes and construct a theoretical framework. 

Findings:  Telemedicine apps, primarily designed for medical management, also enhance tourist safety. However, usability challenges for older users and poor integration with tourism services hinder their adoption. Experts emphasized the importance of accessibility and user-friendly design, while concerns about medical data security were minimal.

Originality/value: This research provides novel insights into the connection of telemedicine and tourism, highlighting
how telemedicine apps can enhance tourist safety and convenience. By integrating expert perspectives, the study offers practical recommendations for tourism stakeholders and app developers to foster innovation and adoption in both sectors.

Research limitations/implications: The findings are based on a small sample size of experts. Future studies could broaden the participant
sample and include actual tourists to gain deeper insights.

Practical implications: Tourism providers should partner with telemedicine developers to enhance tourist safety. Training older users will improve adoption rates. Social implications Integrating telemedicine into tourism can improve access to healthcare, reduce travel-related healthrisks, and promote proactive health management among tourists, benefiting public health. However, the widespread adoption of telemedicine in tourism requires alignment with existing data protection regulations such as the GDPR in Europe and the HIPAA in the United States.

title: Sponsorship Exposure and Short-Term Abnormal Returns: Evidence from Firms Sponsoring Football Clubs under UEFA's New Competition Format in the 2024/2025 Season

detail.title: Sponsorship Exposure and Short-Term Abnormal Returns: Evidence from Firms Sponsoring Football Clubs under UEFA's New Competition Format in the 2024/2025 Season
detail.abstract: The purpose of this paper is to empirically assess whether exposure of a main sponsor's logo on the shirts of clubs competing in UEFA competitions under the new format in the 2024/2025 season translates into a short-term increase in shareholder value for publicly listed sponsor firms and whether the market reaction depends on the sporting context. The study applies an event-study design using daily data. Expected returns are estimated within the Fama-French five-factor model in the estimation window [-250;-30], and abnormal and cumulative abnormal returns are then computed in event windows around match day. Cross-sectional regression analyses indicate that, in the main event window [-2; 3], the highest cumulative average abnormal returns are associated with draws, with similar values for wins and losses. By competition type, the effect is statistically significant in the UEFA Champions League and strongest in the UEFA Europa Conference League, while for the UEFA Europa League it remains statistically ambiguous. Overall, the results support the view that match days under UEFA's new format can generate a short-term price premium for sponsors through an attention and media-exposure channel.

detail.abstract:
The purpose of this study is to examine the differences in fashion purchase behavior among generations in Uzbekistan from 2020 to 2025, especially in terms of brand image, demographic factors, and digital retail platforms. The theoretical framework is based on Generational Cohort Theory and the Technology Acceptance Model. The quantitative research approach is employed in this study, and data is collected from 100 consumers from Generation Z and Millennial generations. The results show that brand image is the most significant predictor of fashion purchase behavior, while e-commerce and social media are also significant but secondary factors in this context. The income level is also found to have a weaker association with fashion purchase behavior.

The results suggest that in transitional emerging markets, brand image and digital retail platforms play a more significant role in determining consumer behavior, especially among younger generations. This study is significant in terms of filling the gap in the existing literature on consumer behavior in Central Asian countries and extends the generational and technology adoption models in the context of a post-Soviet emerging market.

title: Status of the Application of Immersive Technologies in Tourism Research

detail.title: Status of the Application of Immersive Technologies in Tourism Research

publicationDetails.detailsText: Journal of Tourism and Heritage Research (2025), vol.8, nº 4, pp. 36-66

detail.abstract: This study presents a systematic bibliometric analysis of immersive technologies in tourism, focusing on VR, AR and MR. It analyzes 420 publications in Scopus and Web of Science across three periods: VR (1995-2023), AR (2014-2023), and MR (2018-2023). Key metrics examined include publication trends, thematic evolution, journal impact, collaboration networks, and national contributions. VR emerges as the most mature and extensively studied field, with major contributions from China, the UK, and the US. Key themes include destination marketing and tourist satisfaction. AR has seen rapid growth since 2020, particularly in cultural heritage tourism, led by scholars in the UK, China, and Portugal. Increasing attention is directed toward user experience, technology acceptance, and immersive storytelling. In contrast, MR remains underexplored due to technical and cost barriers but show potential for multisensory engagement. Authorship in both VR and AR is fragmented, with a few high-impact teams contributing the majority of output. Research is also geographically imbalanced, with limited contributions from Latin America, Africa, and Southeast Asia. Future research should focus on personalizing immersive experiences and deepening understanding of users' emotional and behavioral responses to VR, AR, and MR. Advancing AR, addressing MR's technical barriers, evaluating long-term impacts, and expanding regional representation are key to enhancing the inclusivity and generalizability of immersive tourism research.

title: Consumers' intention to use bicycle-sharing services: The role of consumer consciousness

detail.title: Consumers' intention to use bicycle-sharing services: The role of consumer consciousness
detail.abstract: A sharing economy enables peer-to-peer (P2P) exchanges of goods and services, benefitting everyone. As traffic congestion and fuel costs continue to rise, bicycle-sharing has gained popularity among citizens as a means of transportation. In recent years, scholars have focused on understanding why people continue to use bicyclesharing. However, little research has combined environmental consciousness, health consciousness, and economic consciousness into one coherent framework. The data for this study was collected from Indian users of bicycle-sharing services. Several factors were examined in explaining bicycle-sharing behavior, including environmental consciousness, economic consciousness, health consciousness, and healthy lifestyle. It was found that consumers' attitudes toward bicycle-sharing services are influenced by a healthy lifestyle, which in turn, mediates the relationship between consumers' health consciousness and attitude toward bicycle-sharing services. The findings of this study can be used to promote sustainable transportation services in the Indian context by government leaders, policymakers, and managers.

title: Navigating Marketing in the Metaverse: A Systematic Literature Review

detail.title: Navigating Marketing in the Metaverse: A Systematic Literature Review
detail.abstract: The growing excitement among practitioners and the surge in academic engagement suggest that the metaverse is poised to impact marketing in the upcoming decades. Over the past two years, there has been remarkable growth in research centered on marketing and the metaverse. Nevertheless, our comprehension of metaverse marketing is still in its early stages and would benefit from a structured and systematic examination demonstrating its effects on consumers. We explored EBSCO, Web of Science, ProQuest, and Scopus to identify 246 articles on the metaverse and marketing. The study utilizes the SPAR-4-SLR framework and draws articles from seventy-nine journals. Our review highlights the theories, contexts, characteristics, and methods (TCCM) that engage scholars. Moreover, the prevailing themes in the literature are identified. An integrative framework, based on the SOR framework, is developed to describe the impact of metaverse marketing on consumers. Finally, a comprehensive and innovative research agenda for future studies is outlined.

title: Unraveling How Multi-Signal Fit Shapes Product Certainty and Purchase Intentions in Live-Streaming Commerce: A PLS-SEM and fsQCA Approach
