detail.title: Unraveling How Multi-Signal Fit Shapes Product Certainty and Purchase Intentions in Live-Streaming Commerce: A PLS-SEM and fsQCA Approach
detail.abstract: In live-streaming commerce, the fit between live-streaming elements and products constitutes a critical external contextual factor shaping consumer decision-making. Prior research has predominantly examined the influence of individual live-streaming elements on purchase intention; however, how the multidimensional fit between these elements and products jointly boosts conversion through cognitive mechanisms remains underexplored. To address this gap, this study synthesizes the signaling and consistency theories into an integrated congruence-signaling framework. Based on survey data collected from 1,207 consumers, this study first employs fuzzy-set qualitative comparative analysis (fsQCA) to identify configurations of live-streaming elements-product fit that enhance product certainty and purchase intention. Partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) was then employed to examine the mechanisms through which these configurations influence product certainty and purchase intention. The results show that product certainty is a necessary condition for high purchase intention and can be achieved through four equivalent pathways, in which product quality and preference certainty act as substitutes. Furthermore, purchase intention is driven by two distinct pathways: streamer-product fit (via consumer-product fit) and danmaku/atmosphere-product fit (via live content-product fit). Both pathways are mediated by product certainty, while streamer-consumer fit moderates their initial stages. These findings provide theoretical grounding and managerial guidance for live-streaming operators seeking to optimize element configurations and enhance sales conversion efficiency.In live-streaming commerce, the fit between live-streaming elements and products constitutes a critical external contextual factor shaping consumer decision-making. title: Channel Erosion at the Retail Terminal: A Game-Theoretic Framework Based on Unmanned Retail
affiliations: Zhongyuan University of Technology, Zhongyuan University of Technology and Zhongyuan University of Technology

detail.title: Channel Erosion at the Retail Terminal: A Game-Theoretic Framework Based on Unmanned Retail
detail.abstract: Against the backdrop of rapid development in internet technology and e-commerce, manufacturers implementing "channel erosion" by establishing direct sales channels has become increasingly common, posing severe challenges to the survival space of traditional retailers. Concurrently, retailer channel innovation models represented by unmanned retail offer new approaches to counter such erosion. However, existing research predominantly focuses on unilateral strategies, either manufacturer erosion or retailer private brand introduction, lacking in-depth exploration of the strategic interaction between manufacturer channel erosion and the introduction of unmanned retail models by retailers. This paper constructs a supply chain game model consisting of a single manufacturer and a single retailer to investigate the strategic interaction mechanism between manufacturer channel erosion and the retailer's introduction of an unmanned retail model. The findings reveal: when facing channel erosion, the retailer's decision to introduce unmanned retail depends on the fixed cost threshold and consumer acceptance; a retailer adopting the unmanned retail model increases the cost of manufacturer erosion; improvements in product quality incentivize strategic innovation for both parties; under the coexistence of manufacturer erosion and retailer unmanned retail, channels form differentiated competition, suppressing wholesale prices while preserving traditional channel value, ultimately achieving supply chain efficiency optimization and maximized consumer welfare. This study integrates manufacturer channel erosion and unmanned retail within a single analytical framework, revealing their strategic defense and interactive relationship, providing new theoretical foundations and managerial insights for supply chain enterprises in channel competition and innovation decisions.

title: Digital Trust and AI-Driven Decision Support Systems in SME Adoption of Mobile Financial Services
affiliations: affiliation not provided to SSRN

detail.title: Digital Trust and AI-Driven Decision Support Systems in SME Adoption of Mobile Financial Services
detail.abstract: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) increasingly adopt artificial intelligence (AI)–enabled mobile financial services within evolving digital commerce ecosystems, yet the role of digital trust in shaping these adoption decisions remains insufficiently understood. Drawing on an decision-making perspective, this study examines how AI utilisation, perceived cybersecurity risk, and system transparency influence SMEs’ adoption of AI-enabled mobile financial services through the mediating mechanism of digital trust.Using a mixed-methods sequential explanatory design, survey data from 127 UK SMEs were analysed using regression and mediation modelling in R and Python, complemented by 16 semi-structured interviews with SME managers and fintech practitioners. The quantitative results indicate that digital trust is the strongest predictor of SME adoption behaviour (β = 0.52, p < 0.001) and perceived financial access (β = 0.44, p < 0.001). AI utilisation positively influences digital trust (β = 0.41), whereas perceived cybersecurity risk negatively affects trust (β = −0.28). System transparency further strengthens digital trust (β = 0.32) and indirectly supports adoption decisions (β = 0.19). Mediation analysis confirms that digital trust fully mediates the relationship between AI utilisation and SME adoption of mobile financial services.Qualitative findings provide additional insight into how SMEs cognitively evaluate AI-generated financial information, highlighting the importance of explainability, reliability, and platform trust in fintech decision-making. The study contributes to electronic commerce and fintech research by demonstrating how digital trust functions as a key cognitive mechanism through which SMEs evaluate and adopt AI-enabled financial technologies within digital financial ecosystems.

title: Build the Medium: Why Organizational Intelligence Is Mechanism, Not Metaphor Working Paper -February 2026

detail.title: Build the Medium: Why Organizational Intelligence Is Mechanism, Not Metaphor Working Paper -February 2026
detail.abstract:
Ten theoretical traditions — from cell biology to thermodynamics to social-systems theory — have independently arrived at the same conclusion about how collective intelligence works, without knowing it. When synthesized, they specify a coherent and mutually reinforcing set of conditions for organizational intelligence that no single tradition could derive alone, and that current enterprise AI strategy does not address.

Every organization already operates through a medium - the informal networks, mentoring relationships, institutional memory, and accumulated ways of working through which judgment propagates and new knowledge emerges. This medium is real but implicit: slow, fragile, confined to human interaction, and invisible to computational systems. We argue that the central task of enterprise AI strategy is to make this existing medium explicit, persistent, and available to computational agents - creating an infrastructure where tacit organizational patterns propagate without full extraction, where agents develop judgment through immersion rather than instruction, and where the organization itself becomes a cognitive system. We propose the Capability x Fertility matrix, showing that current AI maturity frameworks measure capability while systematically underinvesting in fertility - the organizational capacity to generate new value from existing knowledge. Path dependency makes the sequence of investment consequential: organizations that optimize for capability before building fertility face progressively higher costs to add the missing foundation.

Drawing on autopoiesis (Maturana and Varela), scale-free cognition (Levin), the free energy principle (Friston), distributed cognition (Hutchins), social systems theory (Luhmann), absorptive capacity (Cohen and Levinthal), knowledge creation theory (Nonaka and Takeuchi), the adjacent possible (Kauffman), dissipative structures (Prigogine), and hemispheric analysis (McGilchrist), we demonstrate that organizational intelligence is mechanism, not metaphor - the same phenomenon as individual intelligence operating at a different scale. We establish the fertility-first design principle, introduce the distinction between autonomy and initiative as the real measure of AI maturity, and identify the categorical limits of computation that make human participation a permanent design requirement.

This is Paper C of a three-paper programme. Paper A (Reichhart and Gelas, 2026a) diagnoses dynamics blindness as the specific failure mechanism in enterprise AI. Paper B (Gelas and Reichhart, 2026b) specifies the medium's architecture in engineering terms - the tripartite structure of state, dynamics, and agency layers operating on a claims-based knowledge representation with provenance, temporal decay, and competing interpretations. This paper provides the theoretical foundations that explain why that specific architecture is required and what its categorical limits are.

title: The Predictive Organization: Architecture for Enterprise Intelligence Working Paper -February 2026
affiliations: Independent and  Capgemini

detail.title: The Predictive Organization: Architecture for Enterprise Intelligence Working Paper -February 2026
detail.abstract:
JPMorgan Chase runs over 450 AI use cases. Goldman Sachs connects AI to curated market data through a proprietary ontological layer. BlackRock's Aladdin manages over $21 trillion through what functions as an enterprise knowledge graph in all but name. Yet none of these organizations — the best-resourced technology operations in financial services — can answer the question any competent executive asks before making a decision: what happens next? The AI can summarize a risk report but cannot tell you what happens to the risk profile when you change a counterparty's credit limit. Enterprise AI investment is producing capability without organizational intelligence — and the gap is widest in regulated industries where decisions propagate through organizational dependencies and consequences carry legal weight.

This paper specifies an architecture for enterprise intelligence: a tripartite structure consisting of a state layer (the Map), a dynamics layer (the Physics), and an agentic layer (the Player), operating on a claims-based knowledge representation grounded in standardized ontologies. The architecture delivers operational value at each stage of maturity: a queryable dependency map of priority business domains from Phase 1, consequence-tracing "what breaks if" analysis from Phase 2, full scenario simulation from Phase 3, and self-enriching organizational intelligence from Phase 4.

Regulated industries hold a structural advantage they have not yet recognized. Compliance mandates — BCBS 239's data lineage, DORA's dependency mapping, SR 11-7's model governance, the EU AI Act's documentation requirements — already force organizations to build the knowledge infrastructure the architecture requires. The marginal investment to convert static compliance infrastructure into dynamic organizational intelligence is a fraction of the greenfield cost. Organizations that recognize this turn a regulatory burden into a competitive position.

The paper's central intellectual contribution resolves the apparent tension between deterministic traceability and emergent outcomes: drawing on Prigogine's (1980, 1984) dissipative structures, we show that deterministic foundations enable emergence rather than competing with it — stable boundaries do not constrain far-from-equilibrium dynamics but sustain them. We introduce a progressive knowledge stack — ontologies, knowledge graphs, claims with prevalence weighting — as the mechanism through which organizational knowledge remains living rather than archived. This is the second paper in a three-paper programme: the first (Reichhart and Gelas, 2026a) diagnoses dynamics blindness as the failure mechanism; the third (Reichhart and Gelas, 2026c) provides theoretical foundations from complexity science, cognitive science, and social-systems theory.

detail.abstract: In economies characterized by high levels of labor informality and limited access to formal financial services, large segments of the population remain excluded from long-term credit markets-particularly housing finance-despite demonstrating sustained saving capacity. Traditional pension systems and private retirement products are ill-suited to address this exclusion, as they are primarily designed for income replacement in old age rather than for transforming accumulated savings into usable creditworthiness throughout the life cycle. This paper proposes a decentralized, non-custodial framework for voluntary capital accumulation that operates as a credit-enabling financial infrastructure, rather than as a pension or retirement system. By leveraging blockchain technology and smart contracts, individuals can build verifiable and traceable capital positions, along with economic behavior histories, which remain locked under predefined rules but may be contractually committed as conditionally executable guarantees in private credit agreements. Unlike collateralized lending schemes in which assets are transferred or used as a direct source of funding, the accumulated capital in the proposed model is not deployed to finance loans. Instead, it functions as a credible signal of solvency and as an initial layer of risk mitigation, granting execution rights to lenders only in the event of objectively verifiable defaults, through separate guarantee contracts. This architecture preserves user control, avoids custodial intermediation, and reduces discretionary enforcement. The proposed model does not replace public pension systems, does not promise fixed returns, income streams, or retirement benefits, and does not rely on formal employment relationships. Rather, it reframes long-term voluntary saving as an active economic asset capable of reducing information asymmetries, aligning incentives between borrowers and lenders, and expanding access to credit for informal workers, self-employed individuals, and underbanked populations. By explicitly separating capital accumulation from income replacement and embedding it within a programmable, auditable, and legally compatible contractual infrastructure, this approach offers a scalable pathway to improving financial inclusion without introducing systemic risks or competing with existing pension and regulatory architectures. The paper also examines the institutional, regulatory, and operational implications of such systems, as well as their limitations and implementation challenges.

detail.title: The Impact of Digital Redlining in a Post-Pandemic World
detail.abstract: As public spaces, employers, and schools shut down in response to the coronavirus pandemic in March 2020, an issue that librarians and educators were familiar with became evident: the digital divide was alive and well in communities around the world. While historically, the digital divide has been defined since the middle of the 1990s as “the gap between those who do and those who do not have access to new forms of information technology” , two decades later, this definition encompasses information technology such as broadband internet, home computers, stable mobile telephone connectivity and digital television.

title: Towards Knowledge Justice: Centering Marginalized Community Expertise in Academia
affiliations: University of Alberta

detail.title: Towards Knowledge Justice: Centering Marginalized Community Expertise in Academia
detail.abstract: Many Canadian post-secondary institutions currently describe themselves as supporting community-based research, where the work of marginalized community members is valued and integrated into community-based research projects. Our experiences working on sister projects the Sex Work Activist Histories Project (SWAHP) and Eco-systems of Community Research and Recordkeeping (ECRR) have led us to conclude that these institutions in fact often undermine or ignore non-academic knowledges and expertise. University reform is needed to support community-driven research, especially for extremely marginalized communities such as sex workers.

title: Libraries Don't Just Close the Digital Divide -They Redefine Digital Equity
affiliations: Rutgers, The State University of New Jersey - Rutgers University

detail.title: Libraries Don't Just Close the Digital Divide -They Redefine Digital Equity
detail.abstract: While technology is often framed as a great equalizer, access to it remains deeply uneven. The gap is not just about who has Wi-Fi or a laptop. It is about who can fully participate in modern civic, economic, and social life. That is where libraries quietly, but powerfully, step in.

title: Can AI Prompting and Academic Libraries Push the Door of Open Access Wider?
affiliations: Simon Fraser University

detail.title: Can AI Prompting and Academic Libraries Push the Door of Open Access Wider?
detail.abstract: The article argues that skilled AI prompting and academic libraries can work together to widen access to scholarly knowledge. As open access grows, AI can explain and synthesize openly available research for broader audiences. But paywalls still limit what AI can analyze, creating visibility gaps between open and closed scholarship. Libraries help address this by improving institutional repositories, supporting OA publishing through transformative agreements, teaching AI literacy, and developing ethical guidelines. Combined, these efforts make research more accessible, understandable, and useful worldwide.

title: University Libraries: Your Gateway to Citizen Science Success
affiliations: Open University of Sri Lanka and University of Kelaniya, Sri Lanka

detail.title: University Libraries: Your Gateway to Citizen Science Success
detail.abstract: Are you tired up of travelling across the country to various sites for data collection?  Imagine having thousands of eager, geographically distributed volunteers ready to contribute to your research project, and what if these volunteers are people who are already engaged learners, information seekers, and capable of following standard data collection protocols. This resource exists right now in every university library across Sri Lanka.

title: Open Access Boom: Citations Up, Barriers Up
affiliations: Independent

detail.title: Open Access Boom: Citations Up, Barriers Up
detail.abstract: Open Access (OA) publishing has become a major change in how research is shared. In traditional publishing, readers pay to access articles through journal subscriptions. In OA, articles are free to read online right away. This trend has grown fast because many believe it makes science better and fairer. Supporters say OA articles get more citations because more people can read them, leading to greater impact. However, authors often pay high Article Processing Charges (APCs) to publish in OA journals. This creates a debate: Does OA truly boost research impact, or does it create new problems by charging authors large fees?

title: SOS: Dismantle Information Privilege to Save our Science

detail.title: SOS: Dismantle Information Privilege to Save our Science
detail.abstract: The start of this year’s Open Access Week coincided with No Kings demonstrations that took place around the nation on Oct. 18. I found myself that day, as so many of us did, shoulder to shoulder with friends, family and strangers speaking up for democracy. I was at the Seattle Center, at the foot of the Space Needle in downtown Seattle, in a vast crowd, my attention divided between fired-up speakers, inflatable unicorns, posters with wry comments and a rank of flags for veterans for peace. Amid the crowd was a group of intellectual-looking types, most wearing glasses and lab coats, waving SOS banners: Save Our Science. When I saw the SOS signs, I thought about how difficult it is to protect something we can’t see, how difficult it is to convince people of the value of something that they can’t use.

title: Unlocking Access to Information through Plain Language

detail.title: Unlocking Access to Information through Plain Language
detail.abstract: Have you ever been excited to learn something new, but when you started reading about it, you felt completely lost and ended up setting it aside? A large volume of knowledge production is carried out by researchers, who typically convey it using the specialized language of their subject field. This often includes specialized terminology and expressions, acronyms or other abbreviated forms, stylistic conventions, and even particular ways of structuring or formatting a text. The end result is comprehensible to other researchers in the same subject field, but it may be far less accessible to other groups.

title: Redesigning Digital Interfaces for Elderly Users

detail.title: Redesigning Digital Interfaces for Elderly Users
detail.abstract: As we live in a world that is increasingly driven by technology, the problem arises that we are not making these innovations for everyone. According to WHO, the global population of elderly users is expected to double by 2050. The need for more accessible and user-friendly interfaces for elderly users has become increasingly important. The main aim of this research is to explore the challenges faced by elderly users (aged 50 or above) while using digital platforms and to propose solutions to enhance the user experience for elderly users. Using a mixed-methods approach, I conducted a questionnaire, surveys and interviews, and testing with participants from various universities among all age groups. The findings reveal that simple menus, larger text options, clear visuals, and voice assistance can make navigation easier. Allowing users to customize settings to their needs also helps. More importantly, creating easy-to-understand layouts can reduce frustration and build confidence. This study highlights the importance of designing with empathy and keeping elderly users in mind. These findings offer helpful insights for developers and designers to create more accessible and inclusive digital spaces for all ages.

detail.abstract:
Objective: Large-scale observational health datasets often generate high-magnitude health risk signals that are interpreted as immediate hazard warnings. However, the dimensional scale of such data can sometimes lead to a signal inflation where local evidence appears disconnected from broader contextual realities. This study proposes a methodology to verify whether these signals constitute structural artifacts, i.e., stochastic distortions inherent to the spatial architecture of local health repositories. 

Methodology: We present a mathematical framework designed to enhance the reliability of geospatial health surveillance through structural recalibration. By integrating Recentered Influence Function (RIF) regression and a state-tuple formalization, the model anchors local observations to extra-local reference frameworks (e.g., national level standards). Using a spatial Difference-inDifferences (DiD) decomposition, we partition the risk signal into an explained component (linked to local covariates) and a structural unexplained component, effectively isolating the incidence deficit within the data. 

Results: The framework was applied to a massive health dataset. The initial alarm was found to be the byproduct of a 32.5% structural weight deficit in the high-risk stratum and a 45.1% deficit in disease occurrences within the local baseline relative to the national reference. Our modeling demonstrates that this decompositional recalibration is a necessary procedural step for validating large-scale risk assessments. 

Conclusion: By isolating the structural variance between local data and broader benchmarks, this framework ensures higher consistency between dataset-specific outcomes and verifiable reality. It provides a robust tool for decisionmakers to distinguish between genuine health hazards and artifacts of data scale, promoting more accurate global health monitoring.

title: The Double Silence: When Scholarly Publishing Can’t Hear Immigrant Survivors
affiliations: University of Pittsburgh

detail.title: The Double Silence: When Scholarly Publishing Can’t Hear Immigrant Survivors
detail.abstract: In my previous career as a systems librarian, I saw information privilege as a technical problem: who has the password to the database, and who has the funding for the subscription? But as I transitioned into research with Chinese immigrant cancer survivors, I realized that privilege runs deeper than a personal login. Even if we made every medical journal in the world “Open Access” tomorrow, many of the survivors I work with would still be excluded from the conversation. Removing a paywall doesn’t help if the person behind it can’t read the language or can’t find their cultural realities reflected in what counts as evidence.

title: Consumer Engagement with Sequential Content: A Content-Aware Dynamic Choice Model
affiliations: Yale School of Management, Yale School of Management and Yale University

detail.title: Consumer Engagement with Sequential Content: A Content-Aware Dynamic Choice Model
detail.abstract: Sequential content-such as episodic fiction, television series, and online courses-requires consumers to make sequential decisions about whether to continue by incurring access costs or to exit. These choices reflect forward-looking tradeoffs among engagement, delay, and payment, and depend jointly on platform policies and the content encountered along the progression. Yet incorporating high-dimensional content into dynamic choice models remains challenging. We address this by extending adversarial inverse reinforcement learning (AIRL) to accommodate unobserved heterogeneity, identifiable action-dependent utilities, and scalable representations of unstructured content within a structural dynamic framework. We apply the model to 15 months of detailed readership and payment data from a serialized fiction platform. The estimates reveal two dominant segments-Pay & Read and Wait & Read-that account for most consumption and nearly all purchases. Counterfactual analyses show that free access can increase downstream purchases within a user, delay policies can shift engagement toward paid consumption, and content-aware pricing improves monetization while preserving overall usage. More broadly, the paper provides a scalable approach for estimating dynamic choice models with high-dimensional state spaces, offering a tractable framework for studying sequential engagement in modern digital markets.
